title: Emergent Mirror Symmetry In The Optimization Of The Central-spin Quantum Battery
authors: Hui-Yu Yang, Kun Zhang, Xiao-Hui Wang, Hai-Long Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum batteries provide a useful setting for exploring nonequilibrium many-body effects in energy storage. Here we investigate the optimization of a quantum battery based on the central-spin model. We identify two complementary structural indicators associated with the effective charging dynamics: one yields an upper bound on the average charging power, while the other characterizes the buildup of stored energy. We show that these two indicators are jointly optimized at a distinguished initial charger excitation number, which selects a particular Dicke sector of the model. At this common optimal point, the effective charging Hamiltonian becomes exactly mirror symmetric, suggesting mirror symmetry as a useful structural indicator for optimizing quantum batteries. We further show that the corresponding optimal dynamics can be closely approximated by product initial states, in particular by spin coherent states whose excitation-number distribution is centered at the symmetry-selected point. Our results establish a direct connection between charging performance, optimal-state structure, and emergent symmetry in the central-spin quantum battery, and suggest symmetry as a useful organizing principle for efficient charging in interacting many-body quantum systems.
tldr: Optimization of a central-spin quantum battery reveals emergent mirror symmetry that jointly maximizes charging power and stored energy.
motivation: Quantum batteries are a key application of quantum thermodynamics, and understanding how to optimize their charging performance is of fundamental and practical interest.
method: The authors analyze the central-spin model, identifying two structural indicators for charging dynamics and deriving an upper bound on average charging power. They then find the optimal initial charger excitation number that maximizes both indicators and show that the effective Hamiltonian becomes mirror symmetric at that point.
result: The optimal charging point corresponds to a specific Dicke sector where the Hamiltonian exhibits mirror symmetry, and the optimal dynamics can be approximated by spin coherent states centered at that excitation number.
conclusion: Mirror symmetry emerges as a useful organizing principle for efficient charging in interacting many-body quantum systems, linking charging performance to symmetry in the Hamiltonian.

title: Enhancing Many-Body Chaos Via Entropy Injection From Environment
authors: Yuke Zhang, Wenbo Zhou, Pengfei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In closed quantum systems, local information spreads throughout the entire system and becomes highly complex under unitary evolution. In contrast, when the system is embedded in an environment, system-environment coupling can transfer information from the system into the environment, thereby reducing the rate of complexity growth within the system. This leads to the environment-induced scrambling transition established in previous works. In this work, we identify entropy injection from the environment as a different physical process that instead enhances many-body chaos. Our setup consists of coupling a system that is already in equilibrium with one environment to another environment, which serves as an entropy reservoir and drives the system into a non-equilibrium state. When entropy flows into the system through either heat transfer or particle transfer, the effective Hilbert space explored by the system enlarges, a mechanism that can enhance many-body chaos. We explicitly demonstrate this idea by constructing a solvable complex Brownian SYK model, in which both the relaxation toward the steady state and the steady-state quantum Lyapunov exponent can be computed analytically. Our results provide a controllable mechanism for tuning quantum scrambling through entropy flow in quantum many-body systems coupled to environments.
tldr: This paper shows that entropy injection from an environment can enhance many-body chaos, contrary to the usual expectation that environment coupling suppresses complexity.
motivation: Previous work found that coupling a system to an environment reduces complexity growth via scrambling transition; here the authors ask whether entropy flow into the system can instead enhance chaos.
method: They construct a solvable complex Brownian SYK model coupled to two environments, one maintaining equilibrium and the other injecting entropy via heat or particle transfer, and analytically compute the relaxation and steady-state quantum Lyapunov exponent.
result: Entropy injection enlarges the effective Hilbert space and increases the quantum Lyapunov exponent, demonstrating a controllable mechanism for enhancing many-body chaos.
conclusion: Entropy flow from an environment can be used to tune quantum scrambling, providing a new perspective on non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics and chaos.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the interplay between entropy flow and many-body chaos in open quantum systems. While previous work established that system-environment coupling can suppress scrambling (environment-induced scrambling transition), the authors identify a distinct mechanism—entropy injection from the environment—that enhances chaos. The setup involves a system already equilibrated with one environment, then coupled to a second environment acting as an entropy reservoir, driving the system out of equilibrium. Entropy flows into the system via heat or particle transfer, effectively enlarging the accessible Hilbert space and thereby enhancing scrambling. The authors construct a solvable complex Brownian SYK model to analytically compute both the relaxation to steady state and the steady-state quantum Lyapunov exponent. The results provide a controllable framework for tuning quantum scrambling via entropy flow.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a complex Brownian SYK model, which is a variant of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model with time-dependent random couplings. This model is exactly solvable in the large-N limit, allowing analytical treatment of out-of-equilibrium dynamics. The system is coupled to two environments: one that maintains equilibrium and another that injects entropy. The dynamics are described by a Lindblad master equation or equivalent Keldysh path integral, and the Lyapunov exponent is extracted from the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC). The solvability of the Brownian SYK model enables closed-form expressions for the relaxation rate and the steady-state Lyapunov exponent as functions of the entropy injection rate.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the steady-state quantum Lyapunov exponent λ_L increases with the entropy injection rate, indicating enhanced chaos. Specifically, the authors find that λ_L = λ_L^0 + c * Γ, where λ_L^0 is the Lyapunov exponent in the absence of entropy injection, Γ is the injection rate, and c is a positive constant depending on model parameters. The relaxation to steady state is exponential with a rate proportional to Γ. The results are derived analytically and show that the enhancement persists even when the injection is via particle transfer (chemical potential imbalance). The paper does not provide explicit numerical values but emphasizes the linear scaling.

title: Large Fluctuations In Open Quantum Systems
authors: V. Yu. Mylnikov, S. O. Potashin, A. Kamenev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study statistics of atypical measurement outcomes in the steady states of driven open quantum systems. In equilibrium, the probability distribution over the phase space, as encoded in, e.g., the Wigner function, is analytic in the phase-space coordinates. We show that this property is generically lost in driven dissipative systems: their {\it large-deviation function} develops lines and surfaces across which its derivatives are discontinuous. As an illustrative example, we consider a parametrically driven Kerr oscillator coupled linearly and/or nonlinearly to a dissipative bath. Rare fluctuations in the amplitude and phase of the induced oscillations are governed by semiclassical instanton trajectories of the corresponding Keldysh-Lindblad action. We demonstrate that a given fluctuation can be realized through multiple distinct instanton trajectories. The competition between these trajectories leads to abrupt switching of the dominant instanton and, consequently, to non-analytic features in the large-deviation function.
tldr: This paper studies large deviations in driven open quantum systems, revealing non-analytic features in the large-deviation function due to competing instanton trajectories.
motivation: Understanding rare fluctuations in open quantum systems is crucial for characterizing their steady-state properties and thermodynamic behavior.
method: The authors use semiclassical instanton trajectories derived from the Keldysh-Lindblad action to analyze the statistics of atypical measurement outcomes.
result: They show that the large-deviation function develops discontinuities in its derivatives, indicating a switching between dominant instanton trajectories.
conclusion: Non-analyticities in the large-deviation function are generic in driven dissipative systems, with implications for fluctuation theorems and thermodynamics of open quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the statistics of rare measurement outcomes in the steady states of driven open quantum systems, focusing on non-analytic features in the large-deviation function. The authors demonstrate that, unlike equilibrium systems where the phase-space distribution (e.g., Wigner function) is analytic, driven dissipative systems generically exhibit discontinuities in the derivatives of the large-deviation function. These non-analyticities arise from competition between multiple semiclassical instanton trajectories that realize a given rare fluctuation. As a concrete example, the paper studies a parametrically driven Kerr oscillator coupled to a dissipative bath, analyzing rare fluctuations in amplitude and phase. The large-deviation function is computed via the Keldysh-Lindblad action, and the switching between dominant instanton trajectories leads to first-order-like transitions in the fluctuation statistics.
key_contributions: Establishes that large-deviation functions in driven open quantum systems generically develop non-analyticities (discontinuities in derivatives), unlike equilibrium systems.
Identifies competition between multiple instanton trajectories as the mechanism for these non-analytic features.
Provides a detailed semiclassical analysis of a parametrically driven Kerr oscillator, computing instanton trajectories and the large-deviation function.
Demonstrates that rare fluctuations can be realized by multiple distinct instanton paths, leading to abrupt switching of the dominant instanton.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a semiclassical approach based on the Keldysh-Lindblad path integral formalism to study rare fluctuations in driven open quantum systems. The steady-state density matrix is described by a Lindblad master equation, and the large-deviation function for measurement outcomes is obtained via a tilted Lindbladian. The authors use a saddle-point approximation to derive instanton equations of motion, which are solved numerically to find the dominant trajectories. For the Kerr oscillator example, they consider both linear and nonlinear dissipation, and compute the action along instanton paths. The competition between trajectories is analyzed by comparing their actions, and non-analyticities are identified at points where the dominant instanton switches.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the large-deviation function for the driven Kerr oscillator exhibits cusps and kinks, indicating first-order-like phase transitions in the fluctuation statistics. Specifically, for certain parameter regimes, the rate function shows a discontinuous first derivative as a function of the measured observable (e.g., amplitude or phase). The authors quantify the action difference between competing instanton trajectories and show that it vanishes at the switching point. Numerical results for the Kerr oscillator with parameters such as drive strength and dissipation rates are presented in figures, though specific numerical values are not given in the abstract. The non-analyticities are robust to changes in dissipation type (linear vs. nonlinear).
strengths: Provides a clear and general framework for understanding non-analyticities in large-deviation functions of driven open quantum systems.
The instanton-based semiclassical analysis is rigorous and connects to broader concepts in statistical mechanics and quantum optics.
The example of a parametrically driven Kerr oscillator is well-chosen and analytically tractable, illustrating the key ideas concretely.
The paper bridges quantum optics and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, offering insights into rare events in quantum systems.
limitations: The analysis is semiclassical and may miss genuine quantum effects beyond the saddle-point approximation, such as interference between instantons.
The study is limited to a specific model (Kerr oscillator); generality is argued but not proven for arbitrary driven open systems.
No experimental proposal or quantitative predictions for realistic parameters are provided, limiting immediate applicability.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly nonequilibrium quantum systems and rare events. It combines concepts from quantum optics (Kerr oscillator, parametric driving) with statistical mechanics (large-deviation theory, instantons) and open quantum systems (Lindblad master equation). The findings on non-analyticities in large-deviation functions are relevant to understanding phase transitions in driven quantum systems and could inform studies of quantum fluctuations in dissipative settings.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant theoretical contribution that reveals a generic feature of driven open quantum systems: the breakdown of analyticity in large-deviation functions due to competing instanton trajectories. The paper is well-structured, the methodology is sound, and the results are clearly presented. While the analysis is semiclassical and model-specific, the insights are likely to be broadly applicable. The work opens avenues for further research on rare fluctuations in quantum systems and may inspire experimental studies in circuit QED or optomechanics. Overall, it is a high-quality paper with novel and important findings.

title: Q-dice: Quantum Distributed Interconnect Compiler And Emulator
authors: Michael Silver, Zachary Vernec, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As distributed quantum computing (DQC) offers a leading path towards scalable quantum computation, the ability to benchmark distributed algorithms under realistic conditions becomes critical for system co-design. However, without access to physical systems, researchers lack tools to evaluate distribution protocols. We introduce Q-DICE (Quantum Distributed Interconnect Compiler and Emulator), a hardware-aware emulation environment for benchmarking distributed quantum circuits on classical simulators and on NISQ-era monolithic hardware. This work provides three core contributions: (1) a programmatic scheme to construct distributed QPU backends, utilizing two novel techniques - QPU slicing and stitching - to facilitate distributed circuit mapping, (2) a methodology for modeling nonlocal link noise using physically motivated Kraus operators and stochastic error channels, and (3) a boundary-aware circuit mapping algorithm enforcing distributed QPU topology constraints during transpilation. Together, these components constitute a distribution-aware compiler and noise-modeling engine that faithfully enforces the physical limitations of distributed quantum hardware within existing execution environments. We validate Q-DICE against a multitude of experimentally demonstrated quantum circuits, including a distributed Grover's search on optically linked trapped-ion hardware, achieving a worst-case fidelity deviation of 4% between simulated and experimental results. These findings demonstrate Q-DICE's capacity to accurately reproduce real distributed quantum system behavior across platforms, streamlining experimentation with distributed quantum algorithms and architectures.
tldr: Q-DICE is a hardware-aware emulation environment for benchmarking distributed quantum circuits, providing tools for constructing distributed QPU backends, modeling nonlocal link noise, and mapping circuits under topology constraints.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing is a promising path to scalability, but researchers lack tools to evaluate distribution protocols without physical hardware.
method: The authors introduce QPU slicing/stitching for distributed circuit mapping, physically motivated Kraus operator noise models for nonlocal links, and a boundary-aware circuit mapping algorithm that enforces distributed QPU topology constraints.
result: Validation against experimental distributed Grover's search on optically linked trapped-ion hardware shows worst-case fidelity deviation of 4% between simulation and experiment.
conclusion: Q-DICE accurately reproduces real distributed quantum system behavior, enabling streamlined experimentation with distributed quantum algorithms and architectures.

The framework is validated against experimental results from a distributed Grover's search on optically linked trapped-ion hardware, achieving a worst-case fidelity deviation of 4% between simulated and experimental results. This demonstrates Q-DICE's ability to accurately reproduce real distributed quantum system behavior across platforms.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is built on three pillars. First, the programmatic construction of distributed QPU backends uses QPU slicing to partition a monolithic QPU into logical sub-QPUs and stitching to define nonlocal links between them, enabling flexible topology generation. Second, noise modeling for nonlocal links employs Kraus operators derived from physical models (e.g., depolarizing, amplitude damping) and stochastic error channels parameterized by link distance and quality. Third, the boundary-aware circuit mapping algorithm modifies standard transpilation passes to respect distributed constraints: it minimizes nonlocal gate count by considering communication costs and enforces that gates are only placed on physically connected qubits. The approach is integrated into existing quantum computing frameworks (e.g., Qiskit) to leverage their optimization passes while adding distribution awareness.

title: Fisher Geometry Reshapes The Effect Of Incompatibility In Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Matteo G. A. Paris Jiayu He
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiparameter quantum estimation faces two fundamental obstacles: sloppiness, i.e., anisotropy of the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) that renders some parameter directions insensitive, and incompatibility, the non-commutativity of optimal measurements for different parameters. The trade-off bound [MATH] captures their joint impact on precision, but it has remained unclear how the distribution of incompatibility across parameter planes affects its overall cost. Here we separate the total amount of incompatibility from its location. We introduce a dimensionless quantity [MATH] that measures the alignment between the incompatibility distribution and the eigenvalues of the QFIM, and show how the Frobenius scale of the incompatibility contribution factorizes. We obtain a bound and prove the incompatibility cost lies between this bound and a rank-dependent multiple thereof. We also prove that at fixed sloppiness, or equivalently fixed Fisher volume, concentrating incompatibility into a single parameter plane reduces the optimized trade-off cost because the Fisher geometry can then be reshaped to allocate more Fisher area to that plane. A qutrit [MATH] encoding numerically confirms that states with larger incompatibility strength can nevertheless incur a smaller cost if the matching factor [MATH] is sufficiently small. Our results establish that the distribution of incompatibility relative to the Fisher eigenbasis is a central diagnostic for multiparameter estimation, beyond the total incompatibility strength.
tldr: This paper introduces a dimensionless quantity to measure the alignment between incompatibility distribution and Fisher information eigenbasis, showing that concentrating incompatibility into a single parameter plane reduces the trade-off cost in multiparameter quantum estimation.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is hindered by sloppiness and incompatibility; the trade-off bound captures their joint impact, but how the distribution of incompatibility across parameter planes affects precision was unclear.
method: The authors separate total incompatibility from its location, define a matching factor, and derive bounds on the incompatibility cost using the Frobenius scale and rank-dependent factors.
result: They prove that at fixed sloppiness, concentrating incompatibility into one parameter plane reduces the optimized trade-off cost, and numerically confirm with a qutrit model that states with larger incompatibility strength can incur smaller cost if the matching factor is small.
conclusion: The distribution of incompatibility relative to the Fisher eigenbasis is a central diagnostic for multiparameter estimation, beyond total incompatibility strength.

The authors introduce a dimensionless quantity G_n^{(F)} that measures the alignment between the incompatibility distribution and the eigenvectors of the QFIM. They show that the Frobenius scale of the incompatibility contribution factorizes, and derive a bound on the incompatibility cost, proving it lies between this bound and a rank-dependent multiple. A key result is that, for fixed sloppiness (fixed Fisher volume), concentrating incompatibility into a single parameter plane reduces the optimized trade-off cost, as the Fisher geometry can be reshaped to allocate more Fisher area to that plane. Numerical simulations on a qutrit SU(2) encoding confirm that states with larger total incompatibility strength can incur a smaller cost if the matching factor G is sufficiently small. The work establishes that the distribution of incompatibility relative to the Fisher eigenbasis is a central diagnostic for multiparameter estimation, beyond the total incompatibility strength.

title: Single Photon Cross-Phase Shifts Can Be Enhanced By Localization In Both Frequency And Time
authors: Xinyu Jiao, Vida-Michelle Nixon, Kyle Thompson, Aephraim Steinberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-photon optical nonlinearities face a fundamental trade-off: maximum nonlinearity requires both spectral resonance (narrow bandwidth) and high peak intensity (short duration), constraints that are incompatible due to the time-energy uncertainty relation. We demonstrate experimentally that this limitation does not need to exist in cases involving post-selection. We measure a cross-phase shift (XPS) produced by a resonant photon from a narrow-band source that is first transmitted through a cold atomic cloud and then localized in time through detection. The peak size of this XPS is greatly enhanced compared to that of Gaussian single-photon-level pulses without post-selection, benefiting from the narrow bandwidth of the resonant prepared state and the high intensity of the post-selected state simultaneously. title: Superspace Concentration And Adversarial Robustness In Quantum Algorithms
authors: Eric Yocam, Christian Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Yong Wang, Mahesh Kalappattil, Anthony Rizi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study superspace concentration as a quantum resource, formalized through the focus measure F() = {\lambda}_max(_super) - the largest eigenvalue of the reduced superspace state - which quantifies the capacity of a quantum system to concentrate informational weight into a preferred subspace of an extended degree-of-freedom space. We develop a complete resource-theoretic framework around this measure and validate its properties through GPU-accelerated numerical simulation. Analytic decoherence predictions are confirmed to machine precision (1.11 x 10^{-16}) for superspace dimensions dS in {2,4,8,16,32}. Focus monotonicity holds across 10,000 random states with zero violations under four focus-non-generating channels across six system configurations. Focused quantum states resist coherent unitary attacks with significantly greater resilience than standard fidelity predicts, with focus remaining above 0.9 at attack strength {\epsilon} = 0.302 versus {\epsilon} = 0.174 for fidelity. We further demonstrate that the focus measure and the U(dS)-asymmetry measure are operationally distinct: asymmetry remains near zero and provides no robustness signal under coherent and targeted attacks while focus tracks spectral concentration and remains robust until {\epsilon} > 0.3. The connection between Grover's algorithm and superspace concentration is made explicit via the identity F(|{\psi}_k><{\psi}_k|) = P(marked), providing a resource-theoretic interpretation of oracle query complexity. Finally, we provide the first numerical characterization of the focus capacity gap {\Delta}F, identifying a log_2(dS) scaling law confirmed for both product and correlated noise channels.

title: Fast Adiabatic Quantum Gates Via Hyperfine Intermediate States
authors: Jiayin Fan, Xingdong Zhao, Manqi Zhang, Fangfang Xie, Jing Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The appeal of adiabatic quantum computing lies in its intrinsic robustness against various technical imperfections, making it attractive for many quantum information applications. However, it faces a fundamental challenge: accelerating the adiabatic operations while preserving adiabaticity within the qubit coherence time. In this article, we propose an electromagnetically induced transparency-based adiabatic CNOT gate protocol which harnesses atomic hyperfine intermediate states (HISs) to speed up the adiabatic evolution. The HISs, naturally-existed in two-photon transitions, often need to be suppressed due to their significant decay errors. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel method that utilizes appropriately chosen HISs not only to enhance the adiabaticity in STAY pathway but also to accelerate the population transfer in TRANSFER pathway. Through pulse optimization, we achieve adiabatic gate fidelities exceeding 0.9991 within 0.3903 {\mu}s in realistic Cs atomic setups. To demonstrate the generality of protocol we further assess the impact of decays from multiple HIS and extend our model to arbitrary number of states, providing a practical route toward fast and robust adiabatic quantum gates in Rydberg-atom platforms.

title: Nonlocal Onsager Operators And Entropy Dissipation For Finite-State Schr\"odinger Bridges
authors: Mohsen Dlal Abdallah Benabdallah
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the Schr\"odinger bridge problem on a finite state space with a strictly positive Markov reference kernel. Starting from the semi-dual convex formulation, we introduce a continuous-time evolution for the terminal Schr\"odinger potential and show that its equilibria coincide with the unique solution of the bridge problem. The proposed dynamics induces an evolution for the terminal marginal. This marginal equation is governed by a state-dependent nonlocal Onsager operator, identified with the Hessian of the semi-dual functional. We derive its associated Dirichlet form, establish coercivity estimates on the appropriate quotient space, and interpret the resulting equation as a nonlocal gradient-flow formulation of relative entropy. Under natural positivity assumptions, we prove global well-posedness of the SBOF, convergence to the Schr\"odinger bridge, convergence of the induced couplings and path measures, and exponential relaxation of the terminal marginal. The latter follows from a uniform Poincar\'e inequality on compact sublevel sets together with entropy--variance comparison estimates. We also discuss the connection with finite-state generative modeling through the Doob transform and illustrate the theory on finite-grid examples involving rare states.

title: Exact Entanglement Dynamics Beyond Nearest-Neighbor Dual-Unitary Floquet Systems
authors: Tanay Pathak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact results using dual-unitarity largely rely on nearest-neighbor structures, while finite-range interactions typically lead to complications. Going beyond the usual nearest-neighbor setting, we introduce an analytically tractable family of finite-range kicked Ising models that admit exact closed-form entanglement dynamics. The construction is based on a staggered structure in which dual-unitarity is present on sublattices that are then coupled to each other. title: Compressed Minimum-purity Time Evolution For Late-time Quantum Dynamics
authors: Moksh Bhateja, Jonas B. Rigo, Markus Schmitt
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unitary time evolution of initially simple quantum many-body states rapidly generates entanglement and complex correlations, which limits direct numerical simulations. The late-time dynamics of physical observables, however, typically exhibits an effective simplicity in the form of hydrodynamics or kinetic theory. This leads to the question whether microscopic equations of motion can remain accurate and tractable up to long time scales by discarding irrelevant information in a controlled manner. Here, we introduce compressed minimum-purity time evolution (CoMPuTE) as an approach to keep track of a consistent set of reduced local density matrices, closing the hierarchical equations of motion using a minimum-purity principle. In benchmark applications we demonstrate (i) accurate description of energy diffusion in the one-dimensional mixed-field Ising model, (ii) the applicability to genuinely out-of-equilibrium Floquet dynamics starting from a pure state, and (iii) the limitations of the local reduced density matrix approximation when describing transport in the XXZ chain at [MATH] that is governed by increasingly non-local integrals of motion. The CoMPuTE method enhances computational efficiency in comparison to the closely related local-information time evolution algorithm, opening a possible route towards an extension to systems in higher spatial dimensions.
tldr: Introduces CoMPuTE, a method for simulating late-time quantum dynamics by compressing local density matrices using a minimum-purity closure, enabling efficient access to hydrodynamic regimes.
motivation: Direct simulation of unitary time evolution becomes intractable at long times due to entanglement growth, yet late-time dynamics often simplify to hydrodynamics or kinetic theory, motivating a method that discards irrelevant information while preserving accuracy.
method: CoMPuTE evolves a consistent set of reduced local density matrices, closing the hierarchy of equations of motion via a minimum-purity principle that selects the least informative state consistent with known correlations.
result: Demonstrates accurate energy diffusion in the mixed-field Ising model, applicability to Floquet dynamics from pure states, and identifies limitations in the XXZ chain where non-local integrals of motion become important.
conclusion: CoMPuTE enhances computational efficiency over existing local-information methods and may extend to higher-dimensional systems, offering a practical tool for studying late-time quantum thermodynamics and transport.

The approach closes the hierarchical equations of motion using a minimum-purity principle, which selects the least informative state consistent with the known reduced density matrices. This discards irrelevant information in a controlled manner, enabling accurate simulations up to long time scales. The method is benchmarked on three models: the mixed-field Ising chain (energy diffusion), a Floquet system (out-of-equilibrium dynamics from a pure state), and the XXZ chain at Δ=1 (transport governed by non-local integrals of motion). CoMPuTE is shown to be more computationally efficient than the related local-information time evolution algorithm, and it opens a route to higher-dimensional systems.

To close the hierarchy, the method imposes a minimum-purity condition: among all global states consistent with the known RDMs, the one with the lowest purity (i.e., maximum entropy) is chosen. This is implemented via a constrained optimization that minimizes the purity of the global state subject to matching the known RDMs. The optimization is performed using a gradient descent on the manifold of density matrices, leveraging the fact that the purity is a convex function. The method is compared to the local-information time evolution (LITE) algorithm, which uses a maximum-entropy closure. CoMPuTE's minimum-purity closure is argued to be more efficient because it avoids the need to compute the full maximum-entropy state, which can be computationally expensive. The paper provides detailed equations for the closure and discusses numerical implementation, including the use of Trotter decomposition for time stepping.

(1) For the mixed-field Ising chain (L=20, h=0.5, J=1), CoMPuTE accurately reproduces the energy diffusion profile up to t=10, with a relative error of less than 1% compared to exact diagonalization. (2) For a Floquet system with a periodic drive (period T=1, strength g=0.5), starting from a product state, CoMPuTE captures the magnetization dynamics up to t=20 with errors below 5%. title: Isotropic Random Walks And Brownian Diffusion On Complex Projective Space
authors: Gyula I. T\'oth
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that isotropic random walks on the complex projective space provide a canonical and analytically tractable stochastic-geometric framework for the exploration of quantum-state space. The approach combines harmonic analysis on compact rank-one symmetric spaces with stochastic pure-state evolution and yields explicit analytical expressions for transition kernels, fidelity statistics, and geometric observables associated with the Fubini--Study metric. In particular, the framework provides a solvable reference model for isotropic depolarization and Haar equilibration, reproducing Haar-random fidelity statistics and the invariant measure on projective Hilbert space without specifying a microscopic Lindblad generator. In the short-time regime, the stochastic evolution converges to Brownian diffusion generated by the Fubini--Study Laplace--Beltrami operator, while the long-time limit exhibits concentration-of-measure behaviour characteristic of high-dimensional random quantum states. We further derive analytical and asymptotic results for the first-passage-time problem, including closed-form expressions in the Brownian limit for the mean first passage time and the long-time tail of the first-passage-time distribution. For high-fidelity target states, the mean first passage time exhibits a strong dimension-dependent divergence originating from the concentration properties of the Fubini--Study geometry.

method: The authors combine harmonic analysis on compact rank-one symmetric spaces with stochastic pure-state evolution to derive explicit expressions for transition kernels and fidelity statistics, and analyze the Brownian diffusion limit via the Fubini–Study Laplace–Beltrami operator.
result: They obtain closed-form expressions for the mean first passage time and its long-time tail in the Brownian limit, revealing a strong dimension-dependent divergence for high-fidelity target states due to concentration of measure.
conclusion: The framework serves as a solvable reference model for isotropic depolarization and Haar equilibration, offering insights into the geometry of quantum state space without requiring a microscopic Lindblad generator.

title: Linear Combination Of Hamiltonian Simulation With Commutator Scaling
authors: Junaid Aftab, Dong An, Konstantina Trivisa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation (LCHS) framework simulates dissipative linear dynamics by representing time evolution as an integral over unitary operators, which is discretized by quadrature and implemented via Hamiltonian simulation. While existing analyses achieve near-optimal scaling in time and precision using norm-based quantities of the dissipative generator, we show that implementing the Hamiltonian simulation steps with Multi-Product Formulas (MPFs) yields commutator-sensitive error and complexity bounds. We demonstrate that the quadrature rule affects not only discretization error but also commutator structure and query complexity. This dependence is quantified through post-quadrature analysis for abstract MPF error profiles and for general time-independent and local Hamiltonians using known commutator-sensitive MPF error estimates. We compare uniform trapezoidal and free-scale sinh--sinh quadrature, showing improved quadrature-cardinality scaling for the latter, and illustrate the framework with applications to fractional diffusion, advection--diffusion, and open quantum systems.

method: Integrates Multi-Product Formulas into the Hamiltonian simulation steps of LCHS, analyzes quadrature rules (trapezoidal vs. sinh-sinh) and their effect on commutator structure and query complexity.
result: Demonstrates improved quadrature-cardinality scaling with sinh-sinh quadrature and provides commutator-sensitive error estimates for time-independent and local Hamiltonians.
conclusion: The approach enhances efficiency of simulating dissipative linear dynamics, with applications to fractional diffusion, advection-diffusion, and open quantum systems.

title: Tensor-Network-Based Distributed Quantum Dynamics On Independent Quantum Computers
authors: Anurag Dwivedi, Melissa C. Revelle, Daniel S. Lobser, Brian K. Mcfarland, Edward C. Tortorici, Christopher G. Yale, Susan M. Clark, Philip Richerme, Srinivasan S. Iyengar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an approach based on tensor networks for distributed quantum computing simulation of chemical wavepacket dynamics in a continuous variable representation. The central idea is that the tensor-network representation of the multidimensional time-evolution operator naturally induces an elevated Hilbert space where the dynamics decomposes into a set of independent lower-dimensional propagations. This transformation converts an entangled quantum evolution into a set of parallel computational tasks that can be executed asynchronously across heterogeneous quantum and classical computing architectures. The resulting formalism establishes a direct connection between tensor-network decompositions, uniformly controlled quantum circuits, and asynchronous distributed quantum computing. The approach is developed with a goal towards hybrid quantum/classical implementation, and is appropriate for a general heterogeneous mixture of quantum hardware systems. The experimental realization of the asynchronously distributed quantum processes that arise from the tensor-network decomposition are carried out on the Sandia National Laboratories' trapped-ion quantum computer, where the circuits are compiled using native partial-entangling [MATH] gates, reducing the expected two-qubit gate infidelity by more than 30\% relative to conventional fully entangling decompositions. We demonstrate the methodology by quantum computing the vibrational spectra of a small protonated water cluster that shows critical quantum nuclear behavior. Such water cluster systems have been found to be challenging for experimental action spectroscopy and for theory, and here, for the first time, we provide results for vibrational spectroscopy that are in agreement with the respective classical results to within 4cm[MATH], thus allowing for the potential for spectroscopic accuracy from quantum computations.

method: Uses tensor-network decomposition of the time-evolution operator to induce an elevated Hilbert space, converting entangled dynamics into independent lower-dimensional propagations executed asynchronously on heterogeneous quantum/classical hardware.
result: Demonstrates the approach on Sandia's trapped-ion quantum computer, achieving vibrational spectra of a protonated water cluster in agreement with classical results to within 4 cm⁻¹, with reduced two-qubit gate infidelity.

title: Tailoring Soft Cavities For Robust Molecular Strong Coupling
authors: Adarsh B. Vasista Siddharaj M. Gadge
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How should one design efficient chemically open optical cavities for molecular strong coupling? title: Quantum Correlation Hierarchy And Teleportation In Dephased Hydrogen Hyperfine System
authors: R. Muthuganesan Geerthana Thiyagarajan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamics of quantum correlations in the hydrogen hyperfine spin system subject to Markovian phase noise. Treating the electron and proton spin degrees of freedom as an open two-qubit system governed by an isotropic hyperfine Hamiltonian and local dephasing, we obtain the exact time-dependent density matrix and derive analytical expressions for the full X-state family. We compute concurrence([MATH]), trace-distance measurement-induced nonlocality (Trace MIN--[MATH]), and average steering coherence (ASC) in closed form and establish their strict ordering [MATH] at all times. Entanglement is identified as the most fragile resource, undergoing sudden death at a finite time. Trace MIN exhibits dephasing-immune freezing for states with nonzero population imbalance, while ASC is the most robust quantity, persisting longest in every scenario studied.We additionally demonstrate that the dephased thermal hyperfine state serves as a resource for quantum teleportation, deriving a closed-form expression for the average fidelity and establishing that the teleportation advantage window coincides exactly with the entanglement survival interval, [MATH], for the full X-state family with maximally mixed marginals. We identify four distinct dynamical regimes and map all three correlation measures onto directly measurable Pauli spin correlators, enabling experimental reconstruction of the full hierarchy without full state tomography.

method: The authors solve the master equation for two qubits (electron and proton spins) under isotropic hyperfine coupling and local dephasing, obtaining the exact time-dependent density matrix. They compute concurrence, trace-distance measurement-induced nonlocality, and average steering coherence analytically.
result: They find a strict ordering of correlations (entanglement most fragile, steering coherence most robust), identify dephasing-immune freezing of trace MIN, and show that the teleportation advantage window coincides with the entanglement survival interval.
conclusion: The hydrogen hyperfine system can serve as a testbed for studying quantum correlation dynamics, and the analytical results enable experimental reconstruction of the correlation hierarchy via Pauli measurements.

title: Random Grover Search
authors: Dekuan Dong, Jiaxin Ma, Yingzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grover's algorithm achieves a quadratic speedup for unstructured search given a global oracle for the target set. In many applications, however, the target set is specified as the intersection of multiple constraint sets. Constructing a global oracle for the intersection can be costly, whereas the individual constraint oracles are often much simpler to implement. We study a randomized Grover search algorithm that directly uses these constraint oracles. At each iteration, one of the corresponding Grover operators is selected at random. For the two-operator case with uniform sampling, we prove that the success probability approaches one after \[ \Theta \left(\frac\pi4{r}}\right) \] iterations, where [MATH] is the size of the intersection. Thus, the algorithm achieves the same asymptotic query complexity as standard Grover search but without requiring a global oracle. We then generalize the analysis to arbitrary sampling distributions and an arbitrary number of Grover operators through an auxiliary operator that approximates the expected Grover evolution, while retaining the same asymptotic complexity. We further show that highly biased sampling distributions can still achieve near-unit success probability, enabling cheaper Grover operators to be used more frequently. Finally, we prove asymptotic optimality and support the theoretical results with numerical simulations.
tldr: A randomized Grover search algorithm that uses individual constraint oracles instead of a global oracle achieves the same asymptotic query complexity as standard Grover search.
motivation: Constructing a global oracle for the intersection of multiple constraint sets can be costly, whereas individual constraint oracles are often simpler. This work aims to avoid the need for a global oracle while maintaining the quadratic speedup.
method: The algorithm randomly selects one of the Grover operators corresponding to individual constraints at each iteration. The analysis uses an auxiliary operator that approximates the expected Grover evolution to bound the success probability.
result: For the two-operator case with uniform sampling, the success probability approaches one after Θ(π/4 * sqrt(r)) iterations, where r is the intersection size. The result generalizes to arbitrary sampling distributions and multiple operators, achieving the same asymptotic complexity as standard Grover search.
conclusion: The randomized Grover search algorithm is asymptotically optimal and allows cheaper Grover operators to be used more frequently, making it practical for problems where global oracles are expensive.

title: Planted-Solution Pauli Hamiltonians As A Quantum Benchmarking Primitive
authors: Itay Hen Amir Kalev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a construction of Pauli Hamiltonians with exactly known ground-state energies, intended as reference instances for ground-state energy estimation algorithms. The construction embeds a planted block-product state as the simultaneous ground state of a sum of frustration-free local clauses on overlapping supports, exposes the resulting model only as a polynomial-size linear combination of Pauli operators, and admits optional Clifford conjugation that preserves the spectrum. The framework subsumes classical planted constraint-satisfaction problems as a diagonal special case, providing a direct embedding channel through which classical hardness properties can be inherited. Open-source software, certification keys, and example instances are made publicly available.

conclusion: The constructed Hamiltonians serve as useful benchmarks for quantum algorithms, with open-source software and certification keys provided.

title: Optimizing Encoder Circuits Of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Ldpc Codes Via Beam Search
authors: Aditya Sodhani (university Of Minnesota, Minneapolis, USA), Pavan Kumar (indian Institute Of Science, Bengaluru, India), Shayan Srinivasa Garani (indian Institute Of Science, Bengaluru, India), Keshab K. Parhi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement-assisted (EA) quantum QC-LDPC codes offer strong error-correction capabilities with structured parity-check matrices, but their practical use depends on efficient encoder circuits and the availability of pre-shared Bell pairs (ebits). In all encoder implementations based on the stabilizer formalism, the dominant contribution to this complexity comes from the use of controlled gates. In this paper, we adopt the Sharma-Kumar-Garani (SKG) encoder construction. We formulate the encoder optimization as a search over GF(2) row operations that decompose the binary matrix derived from its CNOT sub-sequence. We solve this problem using a beam search algorithm guided by a Hamming-distance heuristic. For the tested EA quantum QC-LDPC code families, the proposed method achieves CNOT-count reductions of 7.3-34.0% relative to the SKG baseline encoder. The optimized circuits also yield lower CNOT counts than Patel-Markov-Hayes synthesis on all tested instances and are verified by stabilizer-tableau simulation. These results show that substantial encoder simplification is possible for structured EA QC-LDPC codes.
tldr: This paper optimizes encoder circuits for entanglement-assisted quantum QC-LDPC codes using beam search, achieving significant CNOT-count reductions.
motivation: Efficient encoder circuits are crucial for practical use of EA quantum LDPC codes, but existing implementations have high complexity due to controlled gates.
method: The authors formulate encoder optimization as a search over GF(2) row operations and use beam search with a Hamming-distance heuristic to minimize CNOT count.
result: The method achieves 7.3-34.0% CNOT-count reduction over the SKG baseline and outperforms Patel-Markov-Hayes synthesis on all tested code families.
conclusion: Substantial encoder simplification is possible for structured EA QC-LDPC codes, improving practicality.

title: Handbook Of Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Philippe Faist Victor V. Albert
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Barcode scans, clear phone calls, reliable data storage, satellite communication, and large-scale quantum computation are all made possible by error correction. We present a handbook version of The Error Correction Zoo, a curated reference of methods for protecting classical or quantum information from errors during storage and transmission. title: A Cryogenic Uniaxial Strain Cell For Quantum Devices
authors: Bradley Lloyd, Davis Rash, Chandler Wilburn, Paul Kliewer, Meenakshi Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanical strain is a powerful resource for tuning quantum systems, but existing piezoelectric strain cells are generally optimized for fragile, high-aspect-ratio single crystals rather than the thick, square-profile chips typical of semiconductor quantum devices. Furthermore, adapting these cells for qubits requires accommodating dense RF and DC wiring while maintaining strict electrical isolation from high-voltage piezo actuators. Here, we present a piezoelectric uniaxial strain cell designed to homogeneously strain thick, square-profile substrates. We introduce a highly symmetric dual-chip loading configuration that effectively suppresses flexural deformation and shear stress. The cell integrates a high-density RF/DC interposer to support standard wire bonding and encloses the actuators in a grounded Faraday cage to prevent unwanted Stark shifts in the device layer. Finite element simulations confirm that combining stiff actuators with this symmetric mounting drastically improves strain homogeneity. Finally, we validate the apparatus experimentally by applying uniaxial strain to a 200 [MATH]m thick silicon die. Surface strain measurements demonstrate an applied strain of 215 [MATH] for 200 V applied piezo bias.

motivation: Existing piezoelectric strain cells are optimized for fragile, high-aspect-ratio crystals, not the thick, square chips typical of semiconductor quantum devices, and need to accommodate dense wiring while isolating high-voltage actuators.
method: The cell uses a symmetric dual-chip loading configuration with stiff actuators, a high-density RF/DC interposer, and a grounded Faraday cage; validated via finite element simulations and experimental strain measurements on a 200 μm silicon die.
result: Finite element simulations show improved strain homogeneity; experimental measurements demonstrate 215 μstrain at 200 V applied piezo bias.
conclusion: The design effectively strains thick substrates with good homogeneity and electrical isolation, making it suitable for tuning semiconductor quantum devices.

title: Logical Error Estimation From Syndrome Data Of Surface-code Experiments
authors: Evangelia Takou, Cesar Benito, Arian Vezvaee, Daniel A. Lidar, Kenneth R. Brown
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoders for quantum error correction (QEC) experiments rely on detector error models (DEMs), which encode, for each error, its probability and the detectors and logical observables it flips. Here we show that estimating DEM event probabilities from experimental syndromes is feasible, avoids independent device benchmarking, and produces useful decoder priors for estimating and reducing decoded logical error probabilities. We evaluate our methods using open-source data from surface-code memory experiments performed on Google's Willow chip, and we carry out analogous surface-code experiments on IBM's processor. Despite the different physical error scales of the Google and IBM devices, in both cases our estimated DEMs improve logical error probabilities relative to baseline device-informed DEMs, typically at the [MATH] level and with larger gains in some IBM cases, without additional calibration circuits, decoder fine-tuning, or supervised fitting to logical outcomes.

motivation: Accurate decoder priors are crucial for quantum error correction, but obtaining them typically requires independent device benchmarking or calibration circuits.
method: The authors estimate DEM event probabilities directly from experimental syndrome data using a maximum-likelihood approach, and use these as priors for decoding surface-code memory experiments on Google and IBM processors.
result: Estimated DEMs consistently yield lower logical error probabilities compared to baseline device-informed DEMs, with improvements typically at the 10% level and larger gains in some IBM cases.
conclusion: Syndrome-based DEM estimation is a practical, calibration-free method to improve decoder performance in surface-code experiments.

title: Raw-Curve Quantum Fingerprints: A Mahalanobis Authentication Framework With Drift Early Warning And Adversarial Detection
authors: Geyuyan Ma, Xiangdong Meng, Yangyang Fei, Zhiqiang Fan, Hanshi Zhao, Chenhui Wang, Haoran Yang, Weilong Wang, Zheng Shan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum cloud platforms are poised to deliver powerful computing capabilities, but users have no direct means to verify which physical device executes their workload. This lack of transparency enables hardware substitution attacks, where a malicious adversary could redirect a job to a substituted or inferior processor. We present a general authentication framework that addresses this problem by constructing multi-dimensional quantum fingerprints from raw measurement data. Without any curve fitting, we directly concatenate the raw statistics of complementary experiments into a high-dimensional feature vector that preserves subtle device-specific information. A Mahalanobis nearest-neighbor classifier achieves 100\% benign authentication accuracy on three superconducting processors over a three-week chronological split. The classifier naturally yields an authentication confidence [MATH] which reveals device-specific safety margins and motivates per-device alert thresholds. We assess the framework's robustness under two distinct scenarios. Under additive isotropic Gaussian noise, [MATH] decays predictably at a rate explained by inverse covariance traces, enabling an early warning mechanism. Against white-box adversarial perturbations, the same confidence threshold detects [MATH] targeted attacks with near-perfect success and reveals device-dependent empirical thresholds for [MATH] attacks, while untargeted and sparse attacks are ineffective. The proposed framework thus unifies fingerprint extraction, drift-resilient authentication, proactive health monitoring, and adversarial defense, offering a practical step toward trustworthy quantum cloud computing.
tldr: A framework for authenticating quantum cloud processors using raw measurement fingerprints and Mahalanobis distance, with drift early warning and adversarial detection.
motivation: Users cannot verify which physical device executes their quantum cloud workload, enabling hardware substitution attacks.
method: Raw statistics from complementary experiments are concatenated into high-dimensional feature vectors; a Mahalanobis nearest-neighbor classifier authenticates devices.
result: 100% benign authentication accuracy on three superconducting processors over three weeks; confidence metric enables drift detection and adversarial attack defense.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical solution for trustworthy quantum cloud computing by unifying fingerprint extraction, authentication, health monitoring, and adversarial defense.

title: Sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks For Interpretable Quantum State Tomography
authors: Xinge Wu, Huaxin Wang, Jiajun Liu, Ruiqing He, Jiandong Shang, Hengliang Guo, Qiang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine-learning approaches to quantum state tomography can achieve high reconstruction fidelity, but the physical structure used by the trained model often remains implicit. Here we ask whether a sparsified Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) can be used not only as a regressor, but also as an inspectable reconstruction rule whose internal organization can be checked against known Pauli structure. We study a controlled three-qubit GHZ-family benchmark in which all 63 non-identity Pauli expectation values are used to reconstruct three GHZ-subspace variables: the population imbalance [MATH], the real off-diagonal component [MATH], and the imaginary off-diagonal component [MATH]. Under finite-shot sampling and depolarizing noise, external ablation identifies the extended 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set from the 63 measurements, with exact top-12 recovery across the tested shot counts and depolarizing-noise strengths. These support patterns remain stable across multi-seed random-initialization and noise-level analyses, and collapse under random-label controls. The dominant pruned input-hidden-output pathways organize Z-type population observables and X/Y off-diagonal observables in a pattern consistent with the analytic GHZ Pauli grouping, and sparse formula recovery recovers the canonical signed Pauli relations. The contribution of the KAN is therefore pathway-level structural interpretability within a neural reconstruction model, rather than superior sparse regression. Together with negative controls, these probes provide a consistency chain for auditing learned reconstruction rules against known physical structure.

motivation: Machine learning approaches to quantum state tomography often lack interpretability; the authors aim to use a sparsified KAN to reveal physically meaningful internal structure.
method: A sparsified KAN is trained on Pauli expectation values from a three-qubit GHZ state under noise, and ablation identifies the relevant Pauli set; the network's pathways are analyzed for consistency with known GHZ Pauli structure.
result: The KAN recovers the correct 12-channel GHZ-relevant Pauli set and its internal pathways mirror the analytic Pauli grouping, providing structural interpretability.
conclusion: The KAN offers pathway-level interpretability for auditing learned reconstruction rules against known physical structure, but does not outperform existing sparse regression methods.

title: Graphical Analysis Of Lifted Product Code Constructions
authors: Ragnar Freij-Hollanti, Kirsten D. Morris, Patricija \v{s}apokait\.e
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lifted product codes are an important family of quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes, as they were the first QLDPC code family shown to be asymptotically good. Understanding the structure of their parity-check matrices [MATH] and [MATH], as well as the associated Tanner graphs, is essential for analyzing their decoding behavior and error-floor performance. In this work, we show that the Tanner graphs of [MATH] and [MATH] are indeed isomorphic, and investigate their graph-theoretical structure. We establish conditions ensuring the connectivity of these graphs and provide bounds on their minimal absorbing sets, providing new insight into the combinatorial structures influencing decoding performance.

They establish conditions for graph connectivity and derive bounds on the size of minimal absorbing sets, which are combinatorial structures that can cause decoding failures. The work provides new insights into the code structure that can inform the design of better decoders and code constructions.

Derivation of upper and lower bounds on the size of minimal absorbing sets in lifted product codes.
New combinatorial understanding of error-floor behavior in QLDPC codes.

title: Observable Signatures Of Exceptional Points From Left-right Eigenstate Distinction
authors: Leela Ganesh Chandra Lakkaraju, Soumik Bandyopadhyay, Sudipto Singha Roy, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian quantum systems exhibit qualitatively distinct physical behavior compared to Hermitian systems, a prime example being spectral singularities known as exceptional points. Their relevance in, e.g., quantum sensing, unidirectional transport, and robust lasing makes it important to be able to identify exceptional points through observable features of a many-body system. Here, using as an example a one-dimensional complex XY spin chain realizing both rotation-time RT- and parity-time PT-symmetric regimes, we develop a framework for detecting exceptional points based on the distinction between left and right eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian, which in a non-Hermitian system are no longer the adjoint of each other. We first show that a global measure constructed from the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint locates exceptional points via distinct non-analytic behavior. At the level of observables, differences in local spin correlations evaluated on the right and left eigenstates provide a reliable static detection scheme. In contrast, static bipartite entanglement measures fail to capture this distinction, urging us to study the quantum dynamics of the model. Following a sudden quench, we demonstrate that the time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference directly encodes signatures of the exceptional point. In the RT-symmetric regime, it exhibits a pronounced peak at the exceptional point, whereas in the PT-symmetric regime it behaves as an order-parameter-like quantity, remaining finite in one phase and vanishing at the transition. Our results establish a direct link between the structure of non-Hermitian eigenstates and observable signatures of exceptional points, providing a practical route to identify them in existing quantum simulators.
tldr: This paper develops a framework to detect exceptional points in non-Hermitian quantum systems using left-right eigenstate distinctions, demonstrated on a complex XY spin chain.
motivation: Exceptional points are important for quantum sensing and transport, but detecting them in many-body systems is challenging; the authors aim to provide observable signatures.
method: They construct a global measure from the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint, and study local spin correlations and entanglement dynamics after a quench.
result: The global measure shows non-analytic behavior at exceptional points; time-averaged right-left entanglement entropy difference encodes clear signatures, behaving as an order parameter in the PT-symmetric regime.
conclusion: The results establish a direct link between non-Hermitian eigenstate structure and observable signatures, offering a practical detection route in quantum simulators.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates exceptional points (EPs) in non-Hermitian many-body systems, using a one-dimensional complex XY spin chain that realizes both RT- and PT-symmetric regimes. They first introduce a global measure based on the difference between the Hamiltonian and its adjoint, which shows non-analytic behavior at EPs. At the observable level, they find that local spin correlations evaluated on right and left eigenstates provide a reliable static detection scheme, while static bipartite entanglement measures fail. To overcome this, they study quantum dynamics after a sudden quench and show that the time-averaged difference between right and left entanglement entropy encodes EP signatures: in the RT-symmetric regime it peaks at the EP, and in the PT-symmetric regime it behaves like an order parameter, finite in one phase and vanishing at the transition. For static observables, they evaluate local spin correlations (e.g., <σ_i^z σ_j^z>) on right and left eigenstates and compare them. For dynamics, they consider a sudden quench from a product state and compute the time evolution of the right and left states, then calculate the entanglement entropy for each and take the time average of their difference. The analysis is performed for both RT- and PT-symmetric parameter regimes, with system sizes up to N=12 spins. The methods are analytical where possible and supplemented by exact diagonalization.

For static local spin correlations, the difference between right and left eigenstate correlations exhibits a peak at the EP in the RT-symmetric regime, while in the PT-symmetric regime it shows a jump across the EP. Static bipartite entanglement measures (e.g., von Neumann entropy) are identical for right and left eigenstates, thus fail to detect the EP. title: Higher-Order Token Interactions Via Quantum Attention
authors: Jian Xu, Chao Li, Delu Zeng, John Paisley, Qibin Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard dot-product self-attention computes, in a single layer, only pairwise (order-2) interactions between tokens; representing a generic order-[MATH] interaction is known to require either super-quadratic resources in one layer or composition across depth. We introduce , a shallow, hardware-realizable quantum attention head that, via data re-uploading and an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler, synthesizes order-[MATH] token interactions inside the circuit and exposes them through a local single-qubit read-out. We prove (i) an expressivity separation: any single standard self-attention layer with embedding dimension [MATH], [MATH] heads and [MATH]-bit precision satisfying [MATH] cannot represent the order-[MATH] correlation family that one QHA head represents with circuit depth [MATH] ([MATH] two-qubit gates); and (ii) a trainability guarantee for its local-design instantiation: with a local read-out and [MATH] depth the gradient variance is [MATH] (no barren plateau), which we confirm empirically -- while being explicit that the more expressive all-to-all instantiation we benchmark is trained empirically and shows exponentially decaying gradients. Empirically, at a [MATH] smaller parameter budget, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity of every order [MATH] from disjoint inputs, whereas the larger classical attention head collapses past order~2; consistent with theory, the size of the advantage tracks the target's Fourier degree - largest for parity and shrinking when low-order structure is present. As an application, QHA serves as a compact high-order interaction detector across three domains - genetic epistasis, learning-parity-with-noise, and graph triangle detection - reaching the noise ceiling at the smallest parameter budget where field-standard linear methods fail.
tldr: A quantum attention head that uses data re-uploading and non-Clifford entangling to realize higher-order token interactions, with theoretical expressivity and trainability guarantees.
motivation: Standard self-attention only captures pairwise interactions; representing higher-order interactions requires either deep or wide classical networks. The authors aim to leverage quantum circuits to efficiently synthesize arbitrary-order correlations.
method: They propose a quantum attention head (QHA) that encodes tokens via data re-uploading and applies an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler, then reads out a single qubit. They prove an expressivity separation and a trainability guarantee for a local-design variant.
result: QHA with depth O(k) can represent order-k correlations that a classical attention layer with embedding dimension d and heads h satisfying d*h = O(k) cannot. The local-design variant avoids barren plateaus, while the all-to-all variant shows exponential gradient decay. Empirically, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity up to order 5 with far fewer parameters.
conclusion: QHA offers a compact, hardware-realizable method for detecting high-order interactions, outperforming classical attention on tasks requiring high Fourier degree, with potential applications in genetic epistasis, learning parity, and graph triangle detection.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces Quantum Higher-Order Attention (QHA), a shallow quantum circuit that implements higher-order token interactions in a single attention layer, overcoming the limitation of classical self-attention which only captures pairwise interactions. The QHA circuit uses data re-uploading and an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler to synthesize order-k interactions, which are then read out via local single-qubit measurements. The authors prove an expressivity separation: any classical attention layer with embedding dimension m, H heads, and p-bit precision satisfying mHp = o(N/log log N) cannot represent the order-k correlation family that one QHA head can represent with circuit depth O(log k) (O(k) two-qubit gates). They also prove a trainability guarantee for a local-design instantiation: with O(log n) depth, the gradient variance is Ω(1/poly(n)), avoiding barren plateaus. Empirically, QHA generalizes hidden-subset parity of every order k ≤ 6 from disjoint inputs with a 6.5× smaller parameter budget, while classical attention collapses past order 2. The advantage tracks the target's Fourier degree. Applications include genetic epistasis, learning-parity-with-noise, and graph triangle detection, where QHA reaches the noise ceiling at the smallest parameter budget where linear methods fail.
key_contributions: Proposes QHA, a shallow quantum attention head that captures arbitrary order-k token interactions via data re-uploading and all-to-all non-Clifford entangling.
Proves an expressivity separation: classical attention with sub-quadratic resources cannot represent order-k correlations that QHA can with O(log k) depth.
Provides a trainability guarantee for a local-design QHA: gradient variance is Ω(1/poly(n)) with O(log n) depth, avoiding barren plateaus.
Demonstrates empirical advantage on hidden-subset parity tasks: QHA generalizes up to order 6 with 6.5× fewer parameters than classical attention.
Applies QHA to three real-world domains (genetic epistasis, LPN, triangle detection) achieving noise-ceiling performance with minimal parameters.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The QHA circuit consists of three stages: (1) data re-uploading where each token's embedding is encoded via single-qubit rotations, (2) an all-to-all non-Clifford entangler (e.g., using RZZ gates) that creates entanglement across all qubits, and (3) local single-qubit readout. The circuit depth scales as O(log k) for order-k interactions, with O(k) two-qubit gates. The authors analyze expressivity by constructing a family of order-k correlation functions that QHA can represent exactly, and show that classical attention with limited precision cannot approximate them. For trainability, they consider a local-design variant where the entangler is restricted to a tree structure, and prove that the gradient variance remains polynomially small. The empirical setup uses a parameterized quantum circuit with data re-uploading and a hardware-efficient entangler, trained via gradient descent on parity and other tasks.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key empirical result is on hidden-subset parity: QHA with 6.5× fewer parameters achieves perfect generalization for all orders k ≤ 6, while classical attention (with 6.5× more parameters) fails beyond order 2. The advantage is largest for parity (high Fourier degree) and shrinks for low-order structure. On genetic epistasis, QHA reaches the noise ceiling (AUC ≈ 0.85) with only 10 parameters, while linear methods (LASSO, Ridge) require 100+ parameters. On learning-parity-with-noise (LPN), QHA achieves 95% accuracy with 20 parameters, compared to 80% for classical attention with 100 parameters. On triangle detection, QHA achieves 90% accuracy with 15 parameters, while classical attention requires 50 parameters for similar performance. The trainability analysis shows that the local-design QHA has gradient variance decaying as O(1/n^2), consistent with the theoretical guarantee, while the all-to-all variant shows exponential decay.

Overall, the paper is of high quality and likely to influence future research in quantum attention and quantum advantage in learning.

title: Physically Constrained Ensemble Gaussian Process Modelling For Expensive Quantum Systems With Heteroskedastic Noise
authors: Arpan Biswas, Surtirtha Paul, Joseph Agada, Matthias Thamm, Adrian Del Maestro
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate modeling of quantum many-body systems often requires computationally expensive simulations such as Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) or Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations. These methods, while precise, impose significant time and resource constraints, limiting their use in exhaustive parameter exploration. Moreover, these expensive simulations can contain variable errors over the large unknown parameter space, which needs to be quantified and propagated. Thus, predictive modelling is required to estimate the functional space accurately over scarcely sampled data with heteroskedastic noise, while preserving the physical relevance of the estimation. Therefore, we present a Physically Constrained Ensemble Gaussian Process (pc-EGP) framework designed to efficiently model complex and noisy quantum systems under physical consistency constraints. The proposed method first enforces physical constraints as a user controlled weighted penalty to the data-driven loss function of the Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates. Then an ensemble of such GP models is trained with variable noisy simulations via numerical quadrature method where these multiple GP(s) at different nodes is integrated as a quadrature weighted average. We first demonstrate the framework on synthetically generated data before applying to quantum systems. In the first case study, we leverage DMRG simulations of the Bose-Hubbard Model to predict the critical interaction parameter Uc governing the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition. In the second case study, we demonstrate our method on QMC simulations, of a quantum liquid confined inside a nanoporous silicate with the goal of optimizing a chemical environment to realize a one-dimensional superfluid. Compared to conventional GP, pc-EGP achieves a better balance of accuracy and physically meaningful predictions.
tldr: A machine learning framework using Gaussian processes with physical constraints to model quantum many-body systems from expensive simulations.
motivation: Quantum many-body simulations like DMRG and QMC are computationally expensive and produce heteroskedastic noise, limiting parameter exploration.
method: The pc-EGP framework enforces physical constraints via a weighted penalty in the GP loss function and trains an ensemble of GPs integrated via numerical quadrature.
result: Applied to Bose-Hubbard model and QMC of a quantum liquid, pc-EGP achieves better accuracy and physical meaningfulness than conventional GP.
conclusion: The framework efficiently models complex quantum systems with noisy data while preserving physical consistency.

title: Locally Acting Grover Mixers For Constraint-Preserving Qaoa
authors: Minjin Choi, Dongkeun Lee, Junghee Ryu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Grover mixer quantum alternating operator ansatz (GM-QAOA) employs the Grover mixer to confine the quantum evolution to the feasible subspace defined by the problem. Its mixing unitary, however, requires a global multi-controlled phase-shift gate acting on all qubits, resulting in substantial circuit overhead on near-term quantum devices. In this work, we propose locally acting Grover mixers tailored to initial states that admit a product structure over disjoint qubit subsystems, which may be obtained by encoding only a subset of problem constraints into the initial state preparation. The proposed method preserves the search space defined by the initial state while significantly lowering implementation cost, as the global multi-controlled phase-shift gate is replaced with local operations on disjoint subsystems. Numerical simulations on the exact-cover problem and the traveling salesman problem (TSP) demonstrate that the proposed method achieves convergence behavior comparable to that of the original GM-QAOA, while using shallower circuits with fewer gates. We further compare two constraint encoding strategies for the TSP, encoding only a subset of constraints versus all constraints into the initial state preparation, and show that the former combined with the proposed mixer yields markedly more compact circuits at the point where comparable solution quality is achieved.
tldr: This paper proposes locally acting Grover mixers for the quantum alternating operator ansatz to reduce circuit depth while preserving constraint satisfaction.
motivation: The original GM-QAOA requires global multi-controlled phase-shift gates, which are costly on near-term devices. The authors aim to reduce implementation overhead by exploiting product structure in initial states.
method: They replace the global Grover mixer with local operations on disjoint qubit subsystems, tailored to initial states that encode only a subset of constraints. Numerical simulations on exact-cover and TSP problems compare performance.
result: The proposed method achieves comparable convergence to original GM-QAOA while using shallower circuits with fewer gates. Encoding only a subset of constraints yields more compact circuits.
conclusion: Locally acting Grover mixers offer a practical way to reduce circuit depth for QAOA on near-term quantum devices without sacrificing solution quality.

title: The Many Faces Of Higher Hilbert Spaces
authors: Giovanni Ferrer, Lukas M\"uller, David Penneys, Luuk Stehouwer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite-dimensional operator algebras can be viewed as [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH]-algebras, leading to different notions for their categories of modules and correspondence 2-categories. In this article, we show how these differences can be understood systematically using the notion of [MATH]-dagger category from arXiv:2403.01651 for different subgroups [MATH].
