To do so, we first introduce [MATH]-Hermitian [MATH]-vector spaces using fixed points of a certain [MATH]-action on [MATH]. We then propose criteria for when such pairings are `positive', generalizing the passage from Hermitian vector spaces to Hilbert spaces. Finally, we outline an inductive approach to defining higher Hilbert spaces in arbitrary dimension, suggesting an extension of these ideas beyond the 2-categorical setting.
tldr: This paper develops a categorical framework for higher Hilbert spaces using *-dagger categories and fixed points of group actions, aiming to generalize Hilbert spaces to higher dimensions.
motivation: To systematically understand the different notions of modules and correspondence 2-categories arising from finite-dimensional operator algebras viewed as different types of *-algebras.
method: Introduces *-Hermitian *-vector spaces via fixed points of a group action on a category, and proposes criteria for positivity to generalize the passage from Hermitian vector spaces to Hilbert spaces.
result: Provides a unified categorical perspective on the many faces of higher Hilbert spaces and outlines an inductive approach to defining them in arbitrary dimension.
conclusion: The work extends the concept of Hilbert spaces to higher-categorical settings, but remains abstract and foundational with no direct application to quantum information processing or thermodynamics.

title: Phase And Coherence Retrieval From Near- And Far-field Intensities
authors: Eran Bernstein, Amit Pando, Asher A. Friesem, Nir Davidson
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the coherence properties of complex optical fields is essential for applications ranging from high power laser arrays to quantum coherent systems. Here, we present a new paradigm for coherence retrieval inspired by the Gerchberg Saxton framework, enabling reconstruction of the first order spatial coherence function (mutual intensity) of partially coherent light from intensity measurements in the near and far fields. We introduce two complementary approaches: a four dimensional Tensor GS algorithm that directly reconstructs the mutual intensity with high accuracy, and a Monte Carlo GS variant that significantly reduces computational cost at the expense of controlled approximation. We validated both methods by reconstructing partially coherent fields in simulated linear and ring arrays of up to 600 beams with prescribed Gaussian decaying coherence. Experimentally, we applied the Tensor GS method to a triangular array of 130 coupled lasers with inhomogeneous spatial coherence, achieving good agreement with theory and a root mean square phase error as low as 2pi over 250.
tldr: A method for retrieving the spatial coherence function of partially coherent light from near- and far-field intensity measurements, inspired by the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm.
motivation: Quantifying coherence properties of complex optical fields is important for applications like high-power laser arrays and quantum coherent systems.
method: Two approaches: a four-dimensional Tensor GS algorithm for direct mutual intensity reconstruction, and a Monte Carlo GS variant for reduced computational cost.
result: Validated on simulated linear and ring arrays up to 600 beams and experimentally on a triangular array of 130 coupled lasers, achieving low phase error.
conclusion: The proposed methods enable efficient and accurate coherence retrieval from intensity-only measurements.

title: Rolling Stock Planning Using The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: Ji\v{r}\'i Guth Jarkovsk\'y, Patricia Bickert, Elisabeth Wybo, Martin Leib
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rolling stock planning is a complex optimization problem in railway management that involves assigning physical trains to scheduled trips while minimizing operational costs. In this work, we address a specific instance of this problem featuring 190 trips over two days, subject to constraints such as mandatory maintenance stops. We reformulate the problem as a Maximum-Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem on a graph where nodes represent feasible train cycles. To handle the computational complexity of the large search space, we propose a hybrid divide-and-conquer algorithm. This approach iteratively selects subgraphs and solves the MWIS problem using various solvers, including exact classical methods and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). We evaluate the algorithm's performance by comparing these methods and analyzing the scaling with respect to subgraph size, with QAOA assessed through both classical simulation and execution on a quantum device (IQM Emerald). Our results indicate that increasing the subgraph size generally improves solution quality, demonstrating that the hybrid framework can effectively bridge the gap between polynomial-time approximate solvers and exponential-time exact methods.
tldr: This paper applies the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to a rolling stock planning problem, a combinatorial optimization task in railway management.
motivation: Rolling stock planning is a complex real-world optimization problem that can be reformulated as a Maximum-Weight Independent Set problem, and the authors aim to solve it using a hybrid classical-quantum approach.
method: The problem is decomposed into subgraphs, and each subgraph's MWIS is solved using exact classical methods or QAOA, with QAOA executed on both classical simulators and the IQM Emerald quantum processor.
result: Increasing subgraph size improves solution quality, and the hybrid framework bridges polynomial-time approximate solvers and exponential-time exact methods.
conclusion: The hybrid divide-and-conquer algorithm with QAOA shows promise for large-scale optimization, but the paper focuses on application rather than advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Phase: Pauli Hierarchical Assembly On Subdivided Elements For Quantum-Compatible Operator Synthesis
authors: Caglar Oskay Tillman Philo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficiently decomposing finite element stiffness matrices into the Pauli basis is challenging due to the exponential growth of Pauli strings with problem size. A naive Pauli expansion requires [MATH] operations, where [MATH] denotes the number of degrees of freedom, rendering direct decomposition infeasible for large systems. Existing approaches exploit algebraic sparsity or operator structure but do not incorporate the geometric organization intrinsic to finite element discretizations, and consequently exhibit poor scaling for stiffness matrices. To address this problem, we introduce PHASE, a hierarchical, geometry-aware Pauli decomposition algorithm that leverages recursive mesh partitioning to organize element contributions across multiple spatial scales. PHASE employs a hybrid strategy that combines full- and reduced-space Tensorized Pauli Decomposition with Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform-based aggregation to assemble global Pauli coefficients efficiently. We show that this approach yields a dimension-dependent reduction in the exponential scaling exponent of Pauli assembly asymptotic complexity relative to existing methods, reducing the cost from [MATH] to [MATH] with [MATH] under standard mesh regularity and balanced partition assumptions. These results substantially improve the feasibility of quantum-compatible operator synthesis for large-scale finite element models.
tldr: A geometry-aware Pauli decomposition algorithm for finite element stiffness matrices, reducing exponential scaling for quantum-compatible operator synthesis.
motivation: Naive Pauli expansion of finite element stiffness matrices is infeasible for large systems due to exponential growth of Pauli strings; existing methods ignore geometric structure.
method: PHASE uses recursive mesh partitioning and a hybrid of full- and reduced-space Tensorized Pauli Decomposition with Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform aggregation.
result: Reduces asymptotic complexity from O(exp(n)) to O(exp(α n)) with α < 1 under standard mesh regularity assumptions.
conclusion: The method substantially improves feasibility of quantum-compatible operator synthesis for large-scale finite element models.

title: Mach's Principle In Atomic Transitions
authors: Bibhas Ranjan Majhi Subhajit Barman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the atomic transition probabilities in atom-mirror set-ups that are in circular motion. In one scenario, the atom is in circular motion inside a static cylindrical mirror. In the other scenario, the cylindrical mirror rotates around its central axis while the atom remains static. We report structural similarity in the atomic transition probabilities between these two cases -- these probabilities are equivalent upon interchanging the field frequencies between the two scenarios. We interpret such an observation as a semi-classical phenomenon analogous to the classical Mach's principle.
tldr: The paper studies atomic transition probabilities in rotating atom-mirror setups and finds a structural similarity analogous to Mach's principle.
motivation: To explore a semi-classical analogue of Mach's principle in atomic transitions, comparing scenarios where either the atom or the mirror rotates.
method: The authors calculate transition probabilities for an atom in circular motion inside a static cylindrical mirror and for a static atom inside a rotating cylindrical mirror, using quantum field theory in curved spacetime or accelerated frames.
result: The transition probabilities in the two scenarios are equivalent upon interchanging field frequencies, showing a structural similarity.
conclusion: This equivalence is interpreted as a semi-classical manifestation of Mach's principle, but the work is theoretical and not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Family-Aware Residual Architecture For Predicting Quantum Circuit Simulation Performance
authors: Honjar Xing, Yehong Jiang, Xianbang Wang, Zehua Wang, Zhicheng Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximate tensor-network simulators enable classical simulation of quantum circuits beyond the reach of exact methods, but selecting optimal approximation parameters -- such as bond dimension thresholds -- remains a costly trial-and-error process. We present a family-aware neural architecture that predicts both the minimum approximation threshold required to achieve target fidelity and the expected wall-clock runtime for quantum circuit simulation, given only the circuit's OpenQASM description and execution context. Our key insight is that quantum circuits from different algorithmic families (e.g., QFT, Grover, VQE) exhibit fundamentally distinct simulation cost profiles due to their differing entanglement structures. We employ family-conditioned residual corrections -- additive, family-specific adjustments atop a shared backbone, drawing on established conditional computation techniques -- enabling the model to capture both universal circuit properties and algorithmic nuances. The architecture incorporates a pretrained family classifier (97.5% accuracy) and domain-informed algorithm fingerprint features derived from gate-composition heuristics. Evaluated on circuits spanning 7--130 qubits across 10 algorithm families, our system achieves 79.5% exact threshold accuracy (91.2% within one rung) and [MATH] runtime correlation, with inference completing in approximately 50 ms -- replacing trial-and-error simulation runs that may take minutes to hours. Ablation studies confirm that family-aware modeling provides the single largest performance improvement (+3.2 percentage points), validating the hypothesis that algorithm family is a first-class feature for simulation cost prediction.
tldr: A machine learning model predicts the simulation performance of quantum circuits using family-aware residual corrections.
motivation: Approximate tensor-network simulators require costly trial-and-error to choose optimal parameters; the authors aim to replace this with a fast predictor.
method: A neural architecture with a shared backbone and family-specific residual corrections, trained on circuit features and a pretrained family classifier.
result: The model achieves 79.5% exact threshold accuracy and high runtime correlation, with inference in ~50 ms.
conclusion: Algorithm family is a key feature for simulation cost prediction, and the family-aware architecture significantly improves performance.

title: Ambiguity-Free Inertial Measurement With Multi-Wavelength Atom Interferometry
authors: Wei-Chen Jia, Yue Xin, Ke Shen, Yan-Ying Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: White-light interferometry enables ambiguity-free localization by synthesizing interference envelopes from multiple optical wavelengths, but no analogous capability has been realized for coherent matter waves. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of multi-wavelength atom interferometry, establishing the matter-wave counterpart of white-light interferometry. By exploiting counter-propagating atomic beams as multi-wavelength matter wave sources and synthesizing interference envelopes from their spectral components, we realize inertial measurements based on envelope localization rather than conventional fringe-phase estimation. The resulting multi-scale interferometric response provides ambiguity-free operation, a well-defined rotational scale factor, and reduced sensitivity to initial phase bias. As a proof of principle, we demonstrate simultaneous dual-axis rotation and acceleration sensing and directly resolve the phase ambiguity that fundamentally limits conventional open-loop atom interferometers. We further measure the Earth's rotation with a relative error of 4.3% and a long-term stability of 93 ppm at an averaging time of 15,000 s. Our results establish multi-wavelength atom interferometry as a new paradigm for coherent matter-wave sensing, extending the principles of white-light interferometry to atom optics and opening new opportunities for inertial sensing, geodesy, precision metrology, and inertial navigation.
tldr: Demonstrates multi-wavelength atom interferometry for ambiguity-free inertial sensing, analogous to white-light interferometry.
motivation: Conventional atom interferometers suffer from phase ambiguity in inertial measurements; multi-wavelength approach aims to resolve this.
method: Uses counter-propagating atomic beams as multi-wavelength matter-wave sources and synthesizes interference envelopes from spectral components.
result: Achieves ambiguity-free dual-axis rotation and acceleration sensing, measures Earth's rotation with 4.3% relative error and 93 ppm stability.
conclusion: Establishes multi-wavelength atom interferometry as a new paradigm for coherent matter-wave sensing with applications in inertial navigation and geodesy.

title: Kohn-Sham Models For Encapsulated Two-dimensional Materials
authors: \'eric Canc\`es, David Gontier, Solal Perrin-Roussel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT) models describing the electronic structure of two-dimensional materials placed in a three-dimensional environment, encapsulated between two parallel conducting electrodes. In this geometry, the Dirichlet boundary conditions at the electrodes screen the Coulomb interaction, which becomes effectively short-ranged, of Yukawa type. We prove that some nonlinear Kohn-Sham DFT models are well-posed in this setting, both for periodic materials (such as graphene) and for quasi-periodic materials (such as twisted bilayer graphene and other moir\'e materials for generic incommensurate twist angles).
tldr: This paper studies Kohn-Sham DFT models for 2D materials encapsulated between electrodes, focusing on well-posedness with screened Coulomb interactions.
motivation: To provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for DFT simulations of 2D materials in a realistic 3D environment with conducting boundaries.
method: The authors analyze nonlinear Kohn-Sham DFT models with Yukawa-type screened Coulomb potentials, proving well-posedness for periodic and quasi-periodic materials using functional analysis and PDE theory.
result: They prove that the models are well-posed for both periodic materials like graphene and quasi-periodic moiré materials like twisted bilayer graphene.
conclusion: The work establishes a sound theoretical basis for DFT simulations of encapsulated 2D materials, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multi-pulse Accumulation Of Gas Molecular Coherence Enables Gigahertz Ultrafast Frequency Conversion
authors: Yazhou Wang, Marcello Meneghetti, Ian Davidson, Timothy Bate, J. E. Antonio-Lopez, Qiang Fu, Jaroslaw Rzegocki, Gregory T. Jasion, Rodrigo Amezcua-Correa, Francesco Poletti, Christos Markos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency conversion of ultrafast lasers is fundamentally constrained by the trade-off between pulse energy and repetition rate, limiting access to regimes critical for fundamental science and industry. Here, we demonstrate a frequency-conversion mechanism in which molecular coherence accumulates across ultrafast pulse trains in gas-filled hollow-core fibers. Unlike conventional nonlinear interactions initiated by individual high-energy pulses, this mechanism relies on the collective buildup of coherent molecular oscillations driven by successive pulses. Using this mechanism, we achieve Raman frequency conversion at repetition rates up to 3 GHz with nanojoule pulse energies. The results establish a regime of nonlinear optical interaction governed by coherence accumulation of gas molecular oscillations with broad implications for ultrafast laser science and frequency conversion technologies.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a frequency conversion mechanism using molecular coherence accumulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers, achieving GHz repetition rates with nanojoule pulses.
motivation: To overcome the trade-off between pulse energy and repetition rate in ultrafast frequency conversion, enabling new regimes for science and industry.
method: The authors use multi-pulse trains in gas-filled hollow-core fibers to build up coherent molecular oscillations, achieving Raman frequency conversion at repetition rates up to 3 GHz.
result: They demonstrate efficient frequency conversion with nanojoule pulse energies at gigahertz repetition rates, a regime previously inaccessible.
conclusion: This coherence accumulation mechanism provides a new approach to ultrafast frequency conversion, with broad implications for laser science and technology.

title: Quantum Iterative Approach To The Traveling Salesman Problem
authors: Arturo Rodr\'iguez-Almaz\'an, Guillermo Rivas, Ricardo S. Alonso, Daniela Falc\'o, Mir Amir Hosseini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a classical NP-hard problem in combinatorial optimization, where determining the shortest route among a set of cities becomes computationally prohibitive as the problem size increases. This work explores quantum computing as an alternative approach to address this complexity. Unlike existing methods that primarily rely on quantum annealing, we propose a quantum iterative framework integrating Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) and Grover's search algorithm. Route costs are encoded as quantum phases, enabling QPE to efficiently evaluate them, while Amplitude Amplification, implemented via the Grover-Long algorithm, iteratively refines the solution space toward the optimal route. A proof-of-concept case study on a small-scale TSP instance demonstrates the feasibility of this approach and its potential for scaling to larger optimization problems. Furthermore, under an expectation-based analysis, the algorithm exhibits an expected computational complexity of [MATH] which depends on the error tolerance parameter [MATH]. This estimation omits the initialization term, which we expect future refinements to render subdominant to Phase Estimation.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum iterative algorithm combining Quantum Phase Estimation and Grover's search to solve the Traveling Salesman Problem.
motivation: The Traveling Salesman Problem is NP-hard and classical methods become prohibitive for large instances; quantum computing may offer a speedup.
method: Route costs are encoded as quantum phases, QPE evaluates them, and Amplitude Amplification via the Grover-Long algorithm iteratively refines the solution space.
result: A proof-of-concept on a small TSP instance shows feasibility; expected complexity depends on error tolerance, with initialization assumed subdominant.
conclusion: The approach shows potential for scaling to larger optimization problems, but further refinements are needed to reduce initialization overhead.

title: Geometric Bias In Eigenspace Perturbation Under Random Heterogeneous Noise
authors: Fengkai Liu, Ke Wang, Wanjie Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral methods rely fundamentally on the stability of principal eigenspaces under random perturbations. Classically, this stability is quantified by the Davis-Kahan and Wedin theorems, which bound the eigenspace error using the operator norm of the noise and the relevant spectral gaps. While these worst-case bounds are sharp for arbitrary deterministic perturbations, they can be wasteful in the low-rank signal-plus-random-noise setting, as they fail to capture the fine-grained interaction between the signal geometry and the noise distribution. In this paper, we study the spectral perturbation of signal-plus-noise matrices corrupted by sparse, random noise with an arbitrary, inhomogeneous variance profile. We demonstrate that under heterogeneous noise variances, the empirical eigenvectors suffer a systematic, deterministic geometric bias that is entirely invisible to classical perturbation bounds. By leveraging the Quadratic Vector Equation (QVE) and establishing fine-grained isotropic local laws, we derive near-optimal, non-asymptotic perturbation bounds for the leading eigenspaces in the operator and [MATH] norms. The bounds separate the usual signal-to-noise contribution, stochastic fluctuations, and structured geometric bias terms determined by the alignment between the signal eigenspaces and the row-wise variance profile.
tldr: This paper studies geometric bias in eigenspace perturbation under heterogeneous noise, using random matrix theory and local laws.
motivation: Classical perturbation bounds like Davis-Kahan are worst-case and fail to capture fine-grained interactions between signal geometry and noise distribution, motivating a more precise analysis.
method: The authors leverage the Quadratic Vector Equation (QVE) and establish fine-grained isotropic local laws to derive non-asymptotic bounds for leading eigenspaces.
result: They show that under heterogeneous noise, empirical eigenvectors suffer a systematic deterministic geometric bias invisible to classical bounds, and provide near-optimal perturbation bounds separating signal-to-noise, stochastic fluctuations, and bias terms.
conclusion: The work advances spectral perturbation theory but is primarily a mathematical result in random matrix theory with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Sharpness Characterizes Hill Functions
authors: Marc Stephan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While long treated as empirical fits, Hill functions have been postulated to be the universal Hopfield barrier for sharpness of input-output responses by Martinez-Corral, Nam, DePace, and Gunawardena. A Hopfield barrier is a fundamental limit on how well biological systems can process information without expending energy. Their case rested on numerical findings for Hill coefficients [MATH] and [MATH]. We give a precise formulation and proof of this: measuring sharpness by the supremum of the derivative in semi-log scale, any rational function [MATH] with real coefficients [MATH] has sharpness at most [MATH], with equality if and only if [MATH] is a Hill function with Hill coefficient [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves that Hill functions are the unique rational functions achieving maximal sharpness, as defined by the supremum of the derivative on a semi-log scale.
motivation: Hill functions are widely used in biology to model cooperative binding, and previous work suggested they are optimal for sharpness without energy expenditure. This paper provides a rigorous proof.
method: The author formulates sharpness as the supremum of the derivative in semi-log scale and uses complex analysis and properties of rational functions to derive an upper bound and characterize equality.
result: Any rational function with real coefficients has sharpness at most the Hill coefficient n, with equality if and only if it is a Hill function with that coefficient.
conclusion: Hill functions are indeed the universal Hopfield barrier for sharpness, confirming the conjecture with a precise mathematical proof.

title: Lifted Gabidulin Construction For Ldpc Representations Of Finite Geometry Codes
authors: Andreas Burg Yifei Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite geometry (FG) codes combine the algebraic properties of classical block codes with the iterative belief propagation (BP) decoding ability of low-density parity-check~(LDPC) codes. However, exploiting both advantages in practice is hindered by the fact that the standard incidence matrix between [MATH]-flats and points is dense and contains many short cycles for any flat dimension [MATH]. In this work, we propose to sparsify the decoding matrix based on pencil selection, formulated as a constant-dimension subspace packing problem and solved explicitly using lifted Gabidulin codes. For both affine and projective geometries, sparse parity-check matrices are constructed and verified for FG codes of lengths up to [MATH]. Simulations on four FG codes show no visible error floor and around [MATH]~dB gain over corresponding 5G LDPC codes at a block error rate of [MATH].
tldr: This paper proposes a method to sparsify parity-check matrices for finite geometry LDPC codes using lifted Gabidulin codes, improving decoding performance.
motivation: Finite geometry codes have dense parity-check matrices with many short cycles, hindering belief propagation decoding. The authors aim to construct sparse matrices to enable efficient decoding.
method: The sparsification is formulated as a constant-dimension subspace packing problem and solved using lifted Gabidulin codes to select pencils, yielding sparse parity-check matrices.
result: Sparse matrices are constructed for FG codes up to length 2^16, and simulations show no visible error floor with about 0.5 dB gain over 5G LDPC codes at BLER 10^-3.
conclusion: The proposed construction effectively sparsifies FG code matrices, improving decoding performance without error floors, making them competitive with 5G LDPC codes.

title: Jaguar: Fast Private Cnn Inference With Power-of-Two Homomorphic Arithmetic
authors: Yewon Jeong, Nayoung Jung, Hyeri Roh, Woo-Seok Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid HE/2PC private CNN inference remains bottlenecked by prime-modulus homomorphic arithmetic in convolution and by a precision flow that runs ReLU at doubled bitwidth before invoking a separate truncation protocol. We present Jaguar, a system built on a single design choice--a power-of-two ciphertext ring--that addresses both. The choice enables SPA-Conv, a coefficient-domain convolution kernel that replaces NTT-centric polynomial multiplication with scalar-polynomial accumulation, and an exact ciphertext-side truncation by local right shifts that lets ReLU run directly at the target fixed-point precision and eliminates the post-ReLU truncation protocol. Where NTT remains genuinely useful--at the client, for the single polynomial multiplication during decryption--we recover it through an auxiliary NTT prime, preserving the power-of-two protocol substrate while keeping decryption O(N log N). On ImageNet-scale ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2 with AVX disabled, Jaguar achieves 2.07-3.72x lower end-to-end latency than Cheetah and 2.16-3.36x lower than Rhombus, with 1.16-1.76x lower communication than Cheetah.
tldr: Jaguar is a system for private CNN inference using power-of-two homomorphic arithmetic to improve latency and communication.
motivation: Hybrid HE/2PC private CNN inference is bottlenecked by prime-modulus homomorphic arithmetic and precision flow issues.
method: Jaguar uses a power-of-two ciphertext ring to enable SPA-Conv (scalar-polynomial accumulation) and exact ciphertext-side truncation, avoiding NTT and post-ReLU truncation protocols.
result: On ImageNet-scale models, Jaguar achieves 2.07-3.72x lower latency than Cheetah and 2.16-3.36x lower than Rhombus, with 1.16-1.76x lower communication.
conclusion: Power-of-two homomorphic arithmetic effectively addresses key bottlenecks in private CNN inference.

title: Game-Theoretic Latent Space Alignment For Multi-user Semantic Mimo Communications
authors: Giuseppe Di Poce, Mattia Merluzzi, Emilio Calvanese Strinati, Paolo Di Lorenzo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic communications enable AI-native wireless systems by mapping raw data into compressed task-oriented latent representations. However, independently trained agents often rely on heterogeneous latent spaces and background knowledge, leading to semantic mismatch that degrades mutual understanding and downstream task execution, especially in interferencelimited multi-user wireless networks. This paper investigates distributed latent-space alignment in multi-user semantic MIMO interference networks with cognitive radio constraints. We consider primary users and semantic-aware secondary users sharing the same wireless resources, where secondary agents must simultaneously mitigate interference and align heterogeneous semantic representations. To address this problem, we formulate semantic alignment as a non-cooperative game and derive a closed-form solution for the joint optimization of linear semantic MIMO transceivers under power and interference constraints. Exploiting the structure of the problem, we recast the original matrix valued optimization into a lower-dimensional power-allocation game, leading to an iterative semantic water-filling algorithm. We establish sufficient conditions for existence, uniqueness, and global convergence to a Nash equilibrium, explicitly relating semantic alignment properties and physical-channel interactions. Numerical results assess the performance of the proposed framework, revealing key trade-offs among semantic compression, task performance, and hierarchical spectrum access.
tldr: This paper proposes a game-theoretic framework for aligning latent semantic representations in multi-user MIMO interference networks with cognitive radio constraints.
motivation: Independent training of semantic communication agents leads to heterogeneous latent spaces and semantic mismatch, degrading performance in multi-user wireless networks.
method: The problem is formulated as a non-cooperative game, with a closed-form solution for joint optimization of linear semantic MIMO transceivers under power and interference constraints, recast as a power-allocation game solved via iterative semantic water-filling.
result: Sufficient conditions for existence, uniqueness, and global convergence to a Nash equilibrium are established, linking semantic alignment to physical-channel interactions. Numerical results show trade-offs among semantic compression, task performance, and spectrum access.
conclusion: The proposed game-theoretic approach effectively addresses semantic mismatch and interference in multi-user semantic MIMO networks, providing a distributed solution with convergence guarantees.

title: Numerical Simulations Of The Spread From The Mean Of The Sle And Multiple Sle Dynamics
authors: Vlad Margarint Phillip Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Schramm-Loewner Evolution (SLE) describes a family of fractal curves that arise in the study of the scaling limits of many planar Statistical Physics models. These curves are modeled using the Loewner Differential Equation for the conformal maps [MATH] with a Brownian motion driver. Using Euler's Method, in the current work we performed numerical experiments to study at a fixed time the quantities [MATH] and [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the real part and [MATH] refers to the sample average. These random variables measure the 'spread' of the dynamics from the average behavior at fixed time. One of the scopes of this work is to give numerical predictions for future theoretical investigations on these quantities. When investigating these quantities in the SLE case our experiments predict that the distribution is bimodal when the dynamics started close to the origin, and it can become bell-shaped if the dynamics is started further from the origin. In the second part, we performed experiments for a Multiple SLE model whose driver is Dyson Brownian Motion. Due to singularity in the dynamics of the drivers and the many data points needed, this part is challenging from a computational perspective. In the multiple SLE case, our experiments predict that the distribution is bell-shaped in all cases. In addition, we check the changes in the distributions as we vary the parameter [MATH] in the SLE case and [MATH] in the Multiple SLE case.
tldr: Numerical simulations of Schramm-Loewner Evolution (SLE) and multiple SLE dynamics, studying the spread from the mean of the driving process.
motivation: To provide numerical predictions for the distribution of the spread from the mean in SLE and multiple SLE, which are fractal curves from statistical physics.
method: Euler's method for numerical integration of the Loewner equation with Brownian motion and Dyson Brownian motion drivers.
result: SLE spread distribution is bimodal near the origin and bell-shaped further away; multiple SLE spread is always bell-shaped.
conclusion: The numerical experiments offer predictions for future theoretical work on these quantities.

title: Time-Reversal Characteristic Modes Of Lossy Reciprocal Structures
authors: Chenbo Shi, Jin Pan, Xin Gu, Shichen Liang, Le Zuo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition is developed for reciprocal lossy electromagnetic structures. The formulation is built on a transmit--receive interpretation of reciprocity: the far-field pattern radiated by a mode determines the time-reversed incident field that is optimally matched to couple energy back into that same mode. This physical picture leads to an antilinear characteristic-mode equation whose solutions remain radiation-power orthogonal even in the presence of material loss, lossy loading, or matched absorption. As a result, the modal expansion coefficients directly represent the radiated-power contributions of the corresponding modes and avoid the singular biorthogonal normalization that may arise in nonnormal classical characteristic-mode expansions. Equivalent formulations are derived in the scattering-operator, T-matrix, and method-of-moments (MoM) frameworks, thereby connecting external wave-channel descriptions with current-space and port-excitation descriptions. The proposed modes reduce to classical characteristic modes in the lossless limit. Numerical examples involving a lossy two-sphere system and a loaded folded antenna demonstrate the radiation-power orthogonality, modal-expansion stability, and power interpretability of the proposed decomposition near exceptional points, where classical characteristic-mode expansions become singular or lose their radiated-power meaning.
tldr: Develops a time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition for lossy reciprocal electromagnetic structures, ensuring radiation-power orthogonality even with losses.
motivation: Classical characteristic-mode expansions become singular or lose physical meaning in lossy systems; a new decomposition is needed to maintain orthogonality and power interpretability.
method: Formulates an antilinear eigenvalue problem based on a transmit-receive reciprocity interpretation, and derives equivalent formulations in scattering-operator, T-matrix, and MoM frameworks.
result: The proposed modes remain radiation-power orthogonal under loss, avoid biorthogonal normalization, and reduce to classical modes in the lossless limit; demonstrated on a lossy two-sphere system and a loaded folded antenna.
conclusion: The time-reversal characteristic-mode decomposition provides a stable and physically meaningful modal expansion for lossy reciprocal structures, useful for antenna and scattering analysis.

title: Impact Of Mode Completeness On The Accuracy Of The Coupling Theory Of Quasinormal Modes: A Strict Numerical Demonstration
authors: Can Tao, Junda Zhu, Haitao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coupling theory of quasinormal modes (QNMs) for a coupled system of generally lossy and dispersive optical nanoresonators has been established in a rigorous manner based on the first principle of Maxwell's equations [Phys. Rev. B 102, 045430 (2020)], and can achieve superior computational efficiency and physical intuitiveness compared with full-wave numerical methods if a small set of modes can achieve a high accuracy. The QNMs suffer from an exponential divergence of far field and can form a complete basis inside but not outside the resonator. In the QNM coupling theory (QCT), it is required that the QNMs of each resonator form a complete basis in expanding the scattered field both inside and outside the resonator, which can be achieved by using regularized QNMs (RQNMs). However, a strict numerical demonstration of the impact of the mode completeness of RQNMs on the accuracy of QCT by using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs is still absent. In this paper, we will provide such a numerical demonstration along with an improvement of the QCT and some theoretical demonstrations on a rigorous incorporation of RQNMs into the QCT. The RQNMs are obtained by introducing an equivalent surface current (ESC) encircling the resonator (called ESC-RQNMs) or the perfectly matched layer (PML) surrounding the computational domain (called PML-RQNMs). The numerical example is selected as two one-dimensional resonators of slabs in the extreme coupling case of direct contact, for which a virtually complete basis of RQNMs can be solved either analytically (for ESC-RQNMs) or numerically (for PML-RQNMs). The results show that by using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs, the QCT can achieve a high accuracy in predicting both the source-free eigenmodes and the source-excited scattered field of the coupled system, which is not true if using the incomplete basis of not-regularized QNMs (i.e., physical QNMs).
tldr: This paper numerically demonstrates the impact of mode completeness on the accuracy of the coupling theory of quasinormal modes for optical nanoresonators.
motivation: The coupling theory of quasinormal modes (QNMs) can achieve high computational efficiency, but its accuracy depends on the completeness of the mode basis. A strict numerical demonstration of this dependence using a virtually complete basis was lacking.
method: The authors use regularized QNMs (RQNMs) obtained via equivalent surface current (ESC) or perfectly matched layer (PML) to form a complete basis, and test the coupling theory on two one-dimensional resonator slabs in direct contact.
result: Using a virtually complete basis of RQNMs, the coupling theory achieves high accuracy in predicting eigenmodes and scattered fields, whereas incomplete bases of not-regularized QNMs fail.
conclusion: Mode completeness is crucial for the accuracy of the quasinormal mode coupling theory, and regularized QNMs provide a complete basis that enables accurate predictions.

title: Designed-Source Reductions And A Dual-Purpose Feasibility Band For Semantic Rate-Distortion
authors: Joss Armstrong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The joint rate-distortion framework of Stavrou and Kountouris (IEEE Transactions on Communications 2023) characterises dual-fidelity tradeoffs for semantic communication on stochastic semantic sources. Many task-oriented communication systems instead use designed sources, where the semantic object is a deterministic oracle allocation [MATH] rather than a stochastic quantity given by nature. We isolate the subclass of designed sources under smooth concave utility with assumptions A1, A2 and Euclidean allocation codomain, and restrict the encoder class to deterministic common-category mappings. Within this subclass the SK exponential-tilting decoder and generalised Blahut--Arimoto iteration specialise to conditional-mean decoding and Lloyd--Max stationarity on [MATH]. When the second fidelity is a monotone single-letter distortion, the joint problem stays inside the SK admissible class; the common-category SK rate is lower-bounded by the max of the corresponding Shannon rate-distortion functions, with equality only when the common-category reconstruction is compatible and RDF-optimal. When the second fidelity is aggregate verification, the joint problem leaves the SK single-letter class and admits a constrained-design feasibility band [MATH] of width [MATH] bits in partition cardinality. The reduction and the band are scope statements on the SK apparatus, not modifications to it. A smart-grid economic-dispatch example with a non-technical-loss-detection contrast illustrates the band.
tldr: This paper studies designed-source reductions and a feasibility band for semantic rate-distortion, focusing on deterministic oracles and concave utility, which is far from the user's research interests.
motivation: To extend the joint rate-distortion framework for semantic communication to designed sources with deterministic oracles, and to characterize the feasibility region when the second fidelity is aggregate verification.
method: The paper isolates a subclass of designed sources under smooth concave utility, restricts encoders to deterministic common-category mappings, and specializes the SK exponential-tilting decoder and Blahut-Arimoto iteration to conditional-mean decoding and Lloyd-Max stationarity.
result: For monotone single-letter distortion, the joint problem stays in the SK admissible class and the common-category SK rate is lower-bounded by the max of Shannon rate-distortion functions. For aggregate verification, the problem leaves the single-letter class and yields a constrained-design feasibility band of width in partition cardinality.
conclusion: The reductions and band are scope statements on the SK apparatus, not modifications, and are illustrated with a smart-grid economic-dispatch example.

title: Quantized Stochastic Primal-Dual Methods For Distributed Optimization Under Relaxed Global Geometry
authors: Susmit Sarkar, Abhinav Raghuvanshi, Kushal Chakrabarti, Mayank Baranwal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study distributed optimization with stochastic gradients and finite-bit communication modeled by random (unbiased) quantization. We propose q-PDGD, a quantized stochastic primal-dual method, and analyze it under relaxed global geometry. Under restricted secant inequality (RSI), a constant step-size yields linear contraction to an explicit neighborhood determined by gradient noise, quantization distortion, and network connectivity, while a diminishing step-size achieves O(1/k) convergence without shared-minimizer assumptions. Under Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality, we obtain linear-to-neighborhood convergence in the same stochastic quantized setting. Our results match the best-known centralized stochastic rates in oracle complexity, and are supported by experiments demonstrating the predicted tradeoffs between quantization level, step-size choice, and graph structure.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantized stochastic primal-dual method for distributed optimization under relaxed global geometry conditions.
motivation: Distributed optimization with limited communication and stochastic gradients is important for large-scale machine learning, but existing methods often require strong convexity or restrictive assumptions.
method: The authors introduce q-PDGD, a primal-dual algorithm that uses random unbiased quantization for finite-bit communication, and analyze its convergence under restricted secant inequality (RSI) and Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) conditions.
result: Under RSI, constant step-size yields linear convergence to a neighborhood determined by noise and quantization; diminishing step-size achieves O(1/k) rate. Under PL, linear-to-neighborhood convergence is obtained. Rates match centralized stochastic optimization.
conclusion: The method effectively handles quantization and stochastic gradients in distributed settings, with theoretical guarantees matching centralized performance.

title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis Of Threshold Group Testing
authors: Remco van der Hofstad, Noela M\"uller, Connor Riddlesden
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Threshold Group Testing (TGT) problem in the noiseless and non-adaptive setting, where the objective is to exactly recover a sparse binary vector from pooled tests, using as few tests as possible. In TGT, each test applied to a subset of items returns a positive outcome if the number of 1's (defective items) in that subset meets or exceeds a specified threshold, and has a negative outcome otherwise. We investigate how the complexity of TGT compares to that of Classical Group Testing (CGT), corresponding to the special case of the threshold equal to one, and analyse the impact of increasing the threshold on the required number of tests. Our main contribution is the derivation of a sharp information-theoretic phase transition at [MATH] (non-adaptive) tests for TGT within the constant-column test design. The threshold constant [MATH] is expressed as a function of the prevalence of defectives and the threshold value. Our upper bound is derived under an analytic assumption, and we verify that this assumption is satisfied for a threshold value of 2. The value of [MATH] reveals that TGT on the constant-column design has the same information-theoretic behaviour as CGT in the low-prevalence regime. Yet, strikingly, at higher prevalences, the threshold leads to a significant reduction in the number of tests. On the other hand, we provide evidence that when the asymptotic proportion of defective items is positive, TGT actually becomes strictly harder than CGT (excluding trivial reductions).
tldr: This paper analyzes the information-theoretic complexity of threshold group testing, a combinatorial search problem, and derives sharp phase transitions for the number of tests required.
motivation: Threshold group testing generalizes classical group testing by allowing a threshold for positive test outcomes, which can reduce the number of tests in certain regimes. Understanding its fundamental limits is important for applications like medical testing or quality control.
method: The authors use information-theoretic tools (Fano's inequality, typicality) to derive lower bounds and a combinatorial algorithm (based on constant-column designs) to achieve upper bounds, establishing a sharp phase transition.
result: The threshold constant for the phase transition is expressed in terms of defect prevalence and threshold value. For low prevalence, TGT behaves like CGT, but at higher prevalences, the threshold significantly reduces the required number of tests. However, when the proportion of defectives is positive, TGT becomes strictly harder than CGT.
conclusion: Threshold group testing exhibits a rich information-theoretic landscape, with regimes where it is easier or harder than classical group testing, depending on defect prevalence.

title: Color-Rule-Function Encoding For Combinatorial Memory
authors: Alexander Khitun
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial memory is a class of memory in which information is encoded in the set of paths through a structured mesh. In this work, we introduce a systematic encoding framework, referred to as the Color-Rule-Function (CRF) approach, for representing information in combinatorial memory. The method consists of four key steps: selecting a sequence of paths in the mesh, assigning values (e.g., colors) to each cell, defining a set of rules based on the values encountered along each path, and constructing a Boolean function that determines the state of each path. . The coding procedure is illustrated by several examples. The design space scales of the CRF scale fundamentally faster compared to conventional memory. This apparent advantage arises from the use of rule-based and functional representations but is accompanied by increased hardware complexity. A possible hardware realization of the CRF framework is discussed. Importantly, the hardware overhead can be substantially reduced through the use of customized modules. The examples of the customized design are described in the text. The combination of CRF coding with customized module design may lead to a practical advantage in data storage density. According to the estimates, the data storage density may exceed Exabit per centimeter squared. A key problem that requires further investigation is related to the minimum Hamming distance between an arbitrary target bit sequence and the closest sequence realizable within the CRF framework under fixed hardware constraints.
tldr: This paper proposes a Color-Rule-Function (CRF) encoding framework for combinatorial memory, aiming to achieve extremely high data storage density.
motivation: Conventional memory technologies face scaling limits; combinatorial memory offers a potential alternative by encoding information in paths through a mesh, but lacks systematic encoding methods.
method: The CRF approach selects paths in a mesh, assigns colors to cells, defines rules based on color sequences, and constructs Boolean functions to determine path states; custom hardware modules are designed to reduce overhead.
result: The CRF framework scales fundamentally faster than conventional memory, with estimated data storage density exceeding Exabit per cm², though hardware complexity is increased.
conclusion: CRF encoding combined with customized module design may lead to practical advantages in data storage density, but further work is needed on minimum Hamming distance constraints.

title: Epistemic Fair Division Of Independence Structures
authors: Marcin Anholcer, Maciej Bartkowiak, Bart{\l}omiej Bosek, Jaros{\l}aw Grytczuk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of fair division of indivisible goods with constraints imposed by a prescribed independence structure, that is, a family of subsets of goods closed under taking subsets. As a motivating example, imagine that the goods to be divided are the available connections in a logistic, financial, or social network. The admissible bundle of goods for each agent must correspond to an acyclic set of edges, corresponding to a basic feasible solution to a linear network problem to be solved. Suppose that all agents assign the same value to each good (in the example, the network connections are equally important for every agent) and evaluate each bundle by summing the values of its goods. Is there a fair partition of the goods into such acyclic bundles? Surprisingly, the answer is yes, provided that the number of agents is at least the arboricity of [MATH], and the fairness requirement is envy-freeness up to one good (EF1). The situation becomes more mysterious when agents have arbitrary additive valuations. Our main result guarantees that, in this case, epistemic EF1 partitions always exist, which means that each agent receives an acyclic bundle for which there exists a feasible partition of the remaining goods into acyclic bundles that they do not envy up to one good. We derive this conclusion from a general result for abstract independence structures defined on the sets of goods. We also discuss connections with several conjectures concerning matroids. In particular, we prove that any Hamiltonian matroid partitionable into two independent sets admits an EF1 bipartition with respect to a common monotone valuation. We complement our results with a constructive perspective: we present explicitly two algorithms for computing the fair allocations described above. Finally, we provide illustrative examples to demonstrate these algorithms on specific instances.
tldr: This paper studies fair division of indivisible goods under independence constraints, such as acyclic subgraphs, using combinatorial and algorithmic methods.
motivation: To ensure fair allocation of goods (e.g., network connections) where each agent's bundle must be independent in a given structure, and to guarantee envy-free allocations up to one good.
method: The authors prove existence of epistemic EF1 partitions for arbitrary additive valuations using abstract independence structures, and provide explicit algorithms for computing such allocations.
result: Epistemic EF1 partitions always exist when the number of agents is at least the arboricity of the graph, and for general independence structures, epistemic EF1 partitions exist for any number of agents.
conclusion: The work establishes fundamental fairness guarantees for constrained fair division, with connections to matroid theory and algorithmic implementations.

title: Maximizing Connectivity Of Uplink RIS-Assisted Uav Networks
authors: Shahrokh Valaee Mohammed Saif
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a new approach for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) positioning and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) partitioning to enhance connectivity of uplink RIS-assisted UAV networks. To achieve this, our approach optimizes RIS-aided link selection, RIS partitioning, and UAV positions to maximize network connectivity characterized by its Fiedler value. Meanwhile, it maintains a specific signal-to-interference plus noise ratio (SINR) constraint for user equipment (UE), which is influenced by RIS partitioning and UAV reliability. The network connectivity optimization problem is formulated using the Fiedler value subject to RIS elements allocation and SINR constraints. This problem is a computationally expensive combinatorial optimization, necessitating an efficient iterative approach. In particular, we propose a perturbation method for RIS-aided link selection, and derive a closed-form solution for RIS partitioning, with each partition tailored to optimize SINR for individual UAV. For the given RIS-aided links and RIS partitioning, we then show that the problem of UAV positioning can be formulated as a low complexity semi-definite programming (SDP) optimization problem, which can be solved using off-the-shelf CVX solvers. Our simulations show the potential gain of UAV positioning and RIS partitioning compared to the benchmark schemes from the literature.
tldr: This paper optimizes UAV positioning and RIS partitioning to maximize connectivity in uplink RIS-assisted UAV networks.
motivation: Enhancing connectivity in UAV networks is crucial for reliable communication, especially in dynamic environments.
method: The authors formulate a combinatorial optimization problem using the Fiedler value and SINR constraints, and propose an iterative approach with perturbation for link selection, closed-form RIS partitioning, and SDP for UAV positioning.
result: Simulations show that the proposed method improves network connectivity compared to benchmark schemes.
conclusion: The approach effectively optimizes UAV positions and RIS partitioning to enhance connectivity while maintaining SINR constraints.

title: A Two-Sided Sketching Algorithm For Low-rank Tensor Train Approximation
authors: Gaohang Yu, Yihao Pan, Ailun Jian, Xiaohao Cai
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensor train (TT) decomposition is a powerful method to acquire low-rank tensors. However, the computational process is frequently obstructed by the large-scale matrix singular value decomposition (SVD). The sketching algorithm serves as an efficient data compression technique that can quickly derive low-rank matrix approximations. In this paper, we propose a randomized algorithm to obtain the TT approximation of tensors using a one-pass sketching algorithm and subspace iteration, and offer thorough error-bound and robustness analysis. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: This paper proposes a randomized algorithm for low-rank tensor train approximation using sketching and subspace iteration.
motivation: Large-scale matrix SVD is a bottleneck in tensor train decomposition; sketching offers a way to accelerate the computation.
method: The authors develop a one-pass sketching algorithm combined with subspace iteration to compute TT approximations, and provide error bounds and robustness analysis.
result: Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
conclusion: The proposed randomized algorithm provides a faster alternative for TT decomposition while maintaining accuracy.

title: Stcc: A Unified Source-Channel Semantic Token Coding Framework For Semantic Communications
authors: Zhicheng Bao, Chen Dong, Sen Wang, Long Liu, Nan Ma, Hao Chen, Xiaodong Xu, Yinqiu Liu, Ping Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (JSCC) has emerged as a promising paradigm for overcoming the ``cliff effect" in wireless communications. However, existing Deep JSCC frameworks operate directly on raw analog data such as image pixels rather than the discrete semantic tokens that foundation models require. Moreover, traditional systems employ fixed, hand-designed constellations that treat all tokens equally, leading to catastrophic random errors under channel noise. In this paper, the Semantic Token Codebook Communication (STCC) is proposed as a unified source-channel semantic token coding framework designed to transmit the discrete semantic tokens of foundation models over noisy channels. The core of STCC is the Semantic Token Codec (STC). It accepts discrete tokens as input, which maintains compatibility with foundation models while employing a residual multiple layer perceptron, i.e., MLP-based encoder that learns geometrically structured constellations optimized with a triple-loss objective. This learned mapping forces the channel topology to align with the semantic embedding space, ensuring that channel noise results in topological errors rather than random corruption. This phenomenon is theoretically and empirically characterized, identifying ``Semantic Drift" in symbolic modalities and ``Structural Distortion" in perceptual modalities, where errors shift predictions to semantically or structurally similar tokens. Extensive experiments demonstrate that STCC significantly outperforms traditional systems in low-SNR regimes, effectively converting channel noise into semantic variations without requiring receiver-side modification.
tldr: Proposes a unified source-channel semantic token coding framework for wireless communications using learned constellations.
motivation: Existing deep JSCC methods operate on raw analog data and treat all tokens equally, leading to catastrophic errors under channel noise.
method: Introduces Semantic Token Codec (STC) with a residual MLP encoder that learns geometrically structured constellations via a triple-loss objective, aligning channel topology with semantic embedding space.
result: STCC significantly outperforms traditional systems in low-SNR regimes, converting channel noise into semantic variations without receiver-side modification.
conclusion: The framework effectively bridges semantic tokens and channel coding, improving robustness in noisy wireless environments.

title: Approximation Properties Of Evolutionary Dynamics In Continuous-Time Finite State Space Games
authors: Pietro Grassi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This thesis studies the convergence of finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics to their deterministic mean-field limit in continuous-time finite state space games. We first develop refined ergodic theorems for Markov chains with a single positive-recurrent class, guaranteeing the existence of a unique invariant distribution and almost-sure convergence of time averages. Next, we prove that the mean-field model, described by a system of Lipschitz-continuous ordinary differential equations, admits a unique solution that depends continuously on its initial condition and that constitutes the almost-sure limit for the empirical distributions with fixed policy. Furthermore, we show that every Mixed Stationary Nash Equilibrium of the mean-field game is approximated by a Nash equilibrium of the corresponding [MATH]-player game within an error [MATH] for sufficiently large [MATH]. We finally demonstrate, by Kurtz's theorem, that the empirical state-policy distribution converges in probability to the mean-field trajectory. Numerical simulations conducted in MATLAB confirm the theoretical [MATH] convergence rate in both models across a range of population sizes.
tldr: This thesis studies the convergence of finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics to deterministic mean-field limits in continuous-time finite state space games, with applications to Nash equilibrium approximation.
motivation: To rigorously establish the connection between finite-population stochastic evolutionary dynamics and their mean-field approximations in game theory.
method: Uses refined ergodic theorems for Markov chains, Lipschitz ODE analysis, and Kurtz's theorem to prove convergence of empirical distributions to mean-field trajectories.
result: Proves that the mean-field model has a unique solution, that empirical distributions converge almost surely, and that mixed stationary Nash equilibria of the mean-field game approximate those of finite-player games with error O(1/N).
conclusion: The mean-field approximation is valid for large populations, with numerical simulations confirming the theoretical convergence rate.

title: An Entropy-based Framework For Hybrid Coalitions In Game Theory. Part I: Human Arbitration
authors: Jose M. Amigo Salome A. Sepulveda-Fontaine
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical Game Theory underpins much of AI and multiagent research, but hybrid Human AI systems require a framework in which execution authority can alternate within a digital environment. We introduce NeoGame Theory, an extension of classical Game Theory for hybrid Human AI coalitions operating under Virtual Nature, the algorithmic analogue of classical (physical) Nature. The framework combines a lexicographic coalition utility with a delegation rule based on the Jensen-Shannon divergence between Human and AI policies. Two thresholds define agreement, contextual, and disagreement regions. In the contextual region, execution follows a scenario specific rule. Apart from the theory, in this paper we develop the first regime, Human arbitration, in which the AI learns by observation and frequency matching while the Human retains final execution authority. We establish the axiomatic basis of the framework and characterize a frequency convergence equilibrium, providing the foundation for later extensions and computational validation.
tldr: This paper proposes NeoGame Theory, an extension of classical game theory for hybrid human-AI coalitions using Jensen-Shannon divergence and a delegation rule.
motivation: Classical game theory does not account for hybrid human-AI systems where execution authority can alternate; a new framework is needed.
method: The framework combines lexicographic coalition utility with a delegation rule based on Jensen-Shannon divergence between human and AI policies, defining agreement, contextual, and disagreement regions.
result: An axiomatic basis is established and a frequency convergence equilibrium is characterized for the human arbitration regime.
conclusion: This work provides a foundation for later extensions and computational validation of hybrid human-AI game theory.

title: Introducing An Extensible Open-Source Toolkit Suite For Studying Second Harmonic Generation: A Case Study Of Depleted Pulsed Gaussian Wave Shg
authors: Mostafa M. Rezaee, Mohammad Sabaeian, Alireza Motazedian, Fatemeh Sedaghat Jalil-Abadi, Mohammad Ghadri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) in nonlinear crystals has been extensively investigated, but most existing models still rely on simplifying assumptions. In realistic settings, thermal effects introduce complications that are difficult to capture analytically because the governing equations are highly coupled and nonlinear. Direct experimental characterization is also limited, since studying thermal effects would require spatiotemporal temperature data at every point in the crystal, which is not experimentally accessible. To address these limitations, we have developed a SHG Computational Toolkit Suite, a coordinated collection of independent modeling toolkits that cover different SHG scenarios under various physical conditions. Each toolkit focuses on a particular configuration or coupling mechanism, while the suite as a whole provides well-documented numerical implementations, reproducible workflows, and illustrative examples. Together, this article and the Toolkit Suite provide a coherent infrastructure for computational studies of SHG. It enables researchers to replicate, adapt, and extend our methods without duplicating foundational development efforts, thereby accelerating SHG research and promoting reproducibility.
tldr: This paper presents an open-source computational toolkit suite for simulating second harmonic generation in nonlinear crystals, focusing on realistic thermal effects.
motivation: Existing SHG models rely on simplifying assumptions and cannot capture coupled thermal effects; experimental characterization is also limited.
method: The authors developed a coordinated collection of independent modeling toolkits covering different SHG scenarios, with well-documented numerical implementations and reproducible workflows.
result: The toolkit suite enables researchers to replicate, adapt, and extend SHG simulations without duplicating foundational development efforts.
conclusion: The toolkit accelerates SHG research and promotes reproducibility by providing a coherent computational infrastructure.

title: Direct Observation Of Anisotropic Surface Phonon Polaritons On \alpha-quartz
authors: Ryoga Odawara, Kotaro Shirahata, Aozora Ohi, Shun Hashiyada, Yukio Kawano
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anisotropic surface phonon polaritons (SPhPs) offer extremely strong light confinement and unique light propagation characteristics, particularly on anisotropic polar crystals. Despite the classical importance of \alpha -quartz as a prototypical uniaxial bulk crystal, real-space observation of anisotropic SPhP propagation on \alpha-quartz has remained elusive. In this study, we report the first direct observation of SPhP propagating on an \alpha-quartz surface using scattering-type near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We demonstrate that the dispersion relation and propagation length of SPhPs exhibit remarkable anisotropy depending on the propagation direction relative to the optic axis of \alpha-quartz. Furthermore, we verify that these experimental behaviors agree with theoretical calculations based on the dielectric permittivity tensors. Our results establish \alpha-quartz as a robust, highly promising platform for light-controlling nanodevices and mid-infrared on-chip sensing.
tldr: This paper reports the first direct observation of anisotropic surface phonon polaritons on α-quartz using near-field optical microscopy.
motivation: Anisotropic surface phonon polaritons offer strong light confinement and unique propagation, but real-space observation on α-quartz, a prototypical uniaxial crystal, had not been achieved.
method: The authors used scattering-type near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) to image SPhP propagation on α-quartz and compared with theoretical calculations based on dielectric permittivity tensors.
result: They observed remarkable anisotropy in dispersion and propagation length depending on direction relative to the optic axis, consistent with theory.
conclusion: α-quartz is established as a promising platform for nanophotonic devices and mid-infrared sensing.

title: Dissociative Recombination And Ion-pair Formation In $\mathrm{HeH^+}$ Isotopologues: A Time-dependent Wave-packet Study Including Rotational Coupling
authors: Sifiso Musa Nkambule, Malibongwe Tsabedze, Oscar N. Mabuza, Mbuso K. Matfunjwa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a comprehensive theoretical investigation of dissociative recombination (DR) and resonant ion-pair (RIP) formation in [MATH] isotopologues using time-dependent wave-packet propagation methods. Nuclear dynamics are treated on a set of 23 coupled electronic states, including [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] symmetries, in both adiabatic and strictly diabatic representations, with rotational couplings explicitly included. Reaction cross sections are computed over collision energies ranging from 0 to 50 eV. The results reveal that inclusion of a large manifold of resonant states and rotational couplings significantly enhances the DR cross section relative to earlier theoretical studies. In the diabatic representation, [MATH] states dominate the recombination dynamics, while in the adiabatic representation, [MATH] and [MATH] states contribute significantly at low collision energies. For RIP formation, two different diabatization schemes yield systematically larger cross sections than previous models, highlighting the sensitivity of ion-pair production to electronic coupling structure. Isotopic effects are examined, showing a clear inverse dependence of cross section magnitude on reduced mass. The present results underscore the importance of multi-state coupling and nonadiabatic effects in accurately describing electron-molecule collision processes in primordial and astrophysical plasmas.
tldr: A theoretical study of dissociative recombination and ion-pair formation in HeH+ isotopologues using time-dependent wave-packet methods with rotational coupling.
motivation: To accurately model electron-molecule collision processes in primordial and astrophysical plasmas, where HeH+ is an important species.
method: Time-dependent wave-packet propagation on 23 coupled electronic states in adiabatic and diabatic representations, including rotational couplings.
result: Inclusion of a large manifold of resonant states and rotational couplings significantly enhances DR cross sections; isotopic effects show inverse dependence on reduced mass.
conclusion: Multi-state coupling and nonadiabatic effects are crucial for accurate description of electron-molecule collisions in plasmas.

title: Nonlinearity Reversal In Epsilon-Near-Zero Indium Tin Oxide Driven By Few-Cycle Light Pulse
authors: Mustafa Goksu Ozlu, Colton Fruhling, Ian Hoffman, Jae Ik Choi, Marcello Ferrera, Alexandra Boltasseva, Vladimir M. Shalaev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent breakthrough studies of nonlinearities at extreme pump intensities ([MATH]1 [MATH]) in transparent conducting oxides (TCOs) have rewritten our understanding of the dynamics in these materials. However, exploring TCO dynamics beyond these intensities is prohibited by the damage threshold of the material. In this work, we overcome this problem by using a few-cycle pump laser pulse (sub-8\,fs) to maximize the intensity while keeping the optical fluence below the damage threshold. We observe a reversal in the optical response trend starting at optical pump laser intensities of [MATH]5 [MATH] similar to Segal et al. At the highest pump pulse intensities, we obtain a complete change in the sign of the modulation for both transmission and reflection, producing a full-cycle oscillation of the refractive index modulation within 300\,fs. The amplitude of the sign reversal scales quadratically with the intensity. We therefore propose a simple two-photon absorption (TPA) model to explain the observed behaviour. The TPA, which is normally forbidden by the Pauli blocking, is enabled here by intraband excitations from the lower to the upper non-equilibrium states of the conduction band (CB). Such excitations vacate the states at the bottom of the CB, lifting up the blocking and thus making interband TPA possible. The model is in good agreement with experimental results, capturing the essential trends in the observed data and revealing the dynamics of competing channels caused by the interplay between interband and intraband transitions. This intensity-controlled mechanism could be the key to unlocking new applications of TCOs for time-varying photonics such as photonic time crystals.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear optical dynamics in indium tin oxide under few-cycle laser pulses, observing a reversal in refractive index modulation due to two-photon absorption enabled by intraband excitations.
motivation: To explore nonlinear optical behavior in transparent conducting oxides at extreme pump intensities beyond the damage threshold, which was previously prohibited.
method: Using a few-cycle pump laser pulse (sub-8 fs) to maximize intensity while keeping fluence below damage threshold, and proposing a two-photon absorption model to explain the observed sign reversal.
result: Observation of a complete sign reversal in transmission and reflection modulation, with amplitude scaling quadratically with intensity, and a full-cycle oscillation of refractive index within 300 fs.
conclusion: The intensity-controlled mechanism could enable new applications in time-varying photonics such as photonic time crystals.

title: Above-bulk Dc Kerr Electro-optics At The water/ITO Interface, Resolved With The Pockels Effect
authors: Soichiro Ashikaga, Kazuaki Nakata, Akihiro Okada, Takumi Takayanagi, Kyohei Yamashita, Takayoshi Kobayashi, Eiji Tokunaga
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On a charged interface, broken inversion symmetry permits a large field-linear Pockels response through [MATH]; at the water/ITO interface [MATH] has been reported to reach the [MATH] order. The coexisting third-order DC Kerr term [MATH] -- small in bulk water ([MATH]) -- had not been jointly parameterized with the Pockels term along the fundamental-frequency ([MATH]) electro-optic path. Superimposing an AC modulation and a DC bias in 0.1\,M NaCl mixes the [MATH] contribution with the 1f response through the cross-term [MATH], so that the water refractive-index modulation [MATH] varies linearly with [MATH]; a model-assisted linear fit then determines both terms from a single AC[MATH]DC sweep. At [MATH] vs Ag/AgCl, [MATH] and, under [MATH], the thickness-normalized DC Kerr coefficient [MATH]. Across physically reasonable [MATH] ([MATH]--[MATH]), the interfacial DC Kerr susceptibility reaches [MATH], several-fold above the visible-range bulk-water value. This response is a property of the specific interface, tunable through the choice of electrode, electrolyte, and solvent rather than intrinsic to bulk water. Amid renewed interest in the Kerr response of water (including recent THz-band optical Kerr studies), the method directly probes this DC Kerr term along the [MATH] path and complements SHG/SFG (the [MATH] path).
tldr: This paper measures the DC Kerr electro-optic effect at the water/ITO interface using a combined AC/DC modulation technique.
motivation: To characterize the interfacial DC Kerr response, which is enhanced compared to bulk water, and to separate it from the Pockels response.
method: Superimposing an AC modulation and a DC bias in an electrochemical cell, the cross-term between the Pockels and DC Kerr effects is extracted via a model-assisted linear fit.
result: The interfacial DC Kerr susceptibility is several-fold above the bulk-water value and depends on the specific interface.
conclusion: The enhanced DC Kerr response is a tunable property of the interface, not intrinsic to bulk water, and the method provides a direct probe along the fundamental-frequency electro-optic path.

title: Polarization-Selective Near-Perfect Absorption Via Mie-Type Resonance In Van Der Waals Anisotropic ReS$_2$/$\alpha$-MoO$_3$/Au Heterostructure
authors: Sudipta Saha Shoumik Debnath
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate polarization-selective absorption in a visible-wavelength heterostructure consisting of a ReS[MATH] stripe grating, an [MATH]-MoO[MATH] spacer, and an Au back-reflector using finite-difference time-domain simulations. For an optimized geometry with a grating period of 500 nm, stripe width of 250 nm, and ReS[MATH] thickness of 80 nm, the structure exhibits near-unity absorption of 99.99\% at 650.5 nm under TE-polarized illumination. The resonant field is concentrated near the outer edges of the ReS[MATH] stripe, while absorption power density is localized in the same region, consistent with a localized edge mode. The absorption response depends strongly on polarization, producing a TE--TM resonance separation of 16.2 nm. Replacing either the biaxial ReS[MATH] layer or the anisotropic [MATH]-MoO[MATH] spacer with isotropic equivalents substantially modifies the spectral response and reduces the polarization-dependent wavelength separation. In addition, rotating the crystal orientation of the ReS[MATH]/[MATH]-MoO[MATH] stack shifts both the resonance wavelength and peak absorption without changing the device geometry. The results show that the combination of anisotropic resonator and spacer layers provides an effective means of controlling resonant absorption and polarization selectivity in van der Waals photonic structures.
tldr: This paper studies polarization-selective near-perfect absorption in a van der Waals heterostructure using Mie-type resonances, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To achieve polarization-selective absorption in the visible range using anisotropic 2D materials for photonic applications.
method: Finite-difference time-domain simulations of a ReS2 grating, α-MoO3 spacer, and Au reflector.
result: Near-unity absorption (99.99%) at 650.5 nm under TE polarization, with strong polarization selectivity and tunability via crystal orientation.
conclusion: The combination of anisotropic resonator and spacer layers enables control over resonant absorption and polarization selectivity in van der Waals photonic structures.

title: Exponential Adaptive Smoothing And Importance Sampling For Optimization Of The Conditional Value-at-Risk
